challenges.title: Bikes bring the revenue. Do they bring the profit?

brief.subject: Where does our profit come from?
body: Bikes are most of what we sell, so I plan the buying budget around them. Before next year's plan I want to see each product category on two measures: revenue and profit.
Use every order line in the data. Profit for a line is the line total minus quantity times the product's standard cost.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which category earns the profit, how the margins compare, and what it means for the budget.
facts: Revenue is LineTotal in ADW_Sales_orders_detail (one row per order line, after discounts).
StandardCost sits on ADW_Dim_Product. The category name is two joins away, through the subcategory table.

questions: Which category brings in the most revenue?
What margin does each category earn?
Does the ranking change when you rank by profit instead of revenue?

frame.nudge: Revenue and profit can rank the categories in a different order. What would you need to know about each line besides what it sold for?
tree: Margin = profit ÷ revenue, and each category's share of total profit
hyp: Bikes lead on revenue and on profit.
A small category may earn a much higher margin than bikes.
traps: Cost is per unit, so multiply by OrderQty before you subtract.
Divide profit by revenue for the margin. Do not average the margins of single lines.
Product to category takes two joins (product, subcategory, category). Miss one and the rows multiply or vanish.

tables: One row per order line with quantity and line total.
Standard cost and the subcategory of each product.
Links a product to its category.
Order header; the detail table already has line totals.
Regions are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders_detail: one row per order line. Every other table here is a lookup with one row per key, so the joins do not multiply rows.
Chain: detail → product → subcategory → category.
data.goal: One row per category: revenue, profit and margin %. Then add each category's share of total revenue and total profit.
data.skeleton:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName AS category
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                         -- profit: line total minus quantity x standard cost
     , ...                         -- margin %
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p ON ____
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON ____
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc ON ____
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
data.solution:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName                                   AS category
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)                   AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost) / 1000000.0, 2) AS profit_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost) / SUM(d.LineTotal), 1) AS margin_pct
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p             ON p.ProductID = d.ProductID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON sc.ProductSubcategoryID = p.ProductSubcategoryID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc    ON pc.ProductCategoryID = sc.ProductCategoryID
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: Subtracting the unit cost without multiplying by quantity understates cost on every multi-unit line.
Standard cost here is the current value on the product table. The cost history table would give a more exact answer.

extra_sql.title: Share of revenue vs share of profit (SUM ... OVER () turns each total into a share; feeds the chart)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName AS category
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal) / SUM(SUM(d.LineTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost)
             / SUM(SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_profit
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p             ON p.ProductID = d.ProductID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON sc.ProductSubcategoryID = p.ProductSubcategoryID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc    ON pc.ProductCategoryID = sc.ProductCategoryID
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
ORDER BY pct_of_revenue DESC

metrics: Sum of line total minus quantity × standard cost.

viz_specs.title: Accessories punch above their weight on profit
viz_specs.sub: Share of total revenue and total profit by category, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two shares per category on one scale: grouped bars. The gap between the two bars is the story.

model: Bikes earn the profit: $7.9M of $9.4M in total (85%), on $94.7M of revenue.

Their margin is thin at 8.4%, though. Accessories earn 50% on only 1.2% of revenue, so they make 6.8% of profit. Components are the weak spot: $11.8M of revenue, a 4.2% margin and only $0.49M of profit, less than accessories.
Keep the buying budget on bikes, and look at pricing and cost on components. Check one thing before acting: standard cost is today's value, so the margins would shift a little with the cost history.
checks: I joined all four tables and multiplied cost by quantity.
I compared revenue rank with profit rank.
I used margin and share of profit, not revenue alone.
I named one caveat about cost.

challenges.title: Which sales territory grew fastest in 2013?

brief.subject: Territory growth, 2013 vs 2012
body: I'm splitting next year's sales targets by territory and I want to start from what grew last year. Please compare 2013 with 2012 for each of the ten territories.
Use revenue (SubTotal) and compare full years only.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: who grew fastest, how you measured it, and which territory needs attention.
facts: ADW_Sales_orders has a TerritoryID on each order. Names live in ADW_Dim_Territory.

questions: Which territory grew fastest in percent?
Which territory added the most dollars?
Did any territory shrink?

frame.nudge: A territory that doubled from a tiny base and a territory that added the most dollars are not always the same one. Which of the two matters for setting targets?
tree: Revenue per territory in 2012 and in 2013
Growth in percent and in dollars
hyp: The fastest growers are outside the US.
The biggest percent gain comes from a small starting base.
traps: Filter to the two full years. 2011 and 2014 are partial and would distort the comparison.
Percent growth hides the starting size. Put the dollar gain next to it.
Use >= and < on dates instead of BETWEEN with an end date.

tables: One row per order with date, territory and subtotal.
Line level; the order header already has the subtotal.
Products are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order, so SUM(SubTotal) per territory is safe.
ADW_Dim_Territory: one row per territory, so the join keeps one row per order.
data.goal: One row per territory: revenue in 2012, revenue in 2013, dollar gain and growth %, best first.
data.skeleton:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT t.TerritoryName
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2012 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2012_m
         , ...                                  -- the same for 2013
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
    JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t ON ____
    WHERE ____                                 -- the two full years
    GROUP BY t.TerritoryName
)
SELECT TerritoryName, rev_2012_m, rev_2013_m
     , ...                                      -- gain in $M
     , ...                                      -- growth %
FROM yearly
data.solution:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT t.TerritoryName
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2012 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2012_m
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2013 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2013_m
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
    JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t ON t.TerritoryID = o.TerritoryID
    WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2012-01-01' AND o.OrderDate < '2014-01-01'
    GROUP BY t.TerritoryName
)
SELECT TerritoryName
     , ROUND(rev_2012_m, 2)                                 AS rev_2012_m
     , ROUND(rev_2013_m, 2)                                 AS rev_2013_m
     , ROUND(rev_2013_m - rev_2012_m, 2)                    AS gain_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * (rev_2013_m - rev_2012_m) / rev_2012_m, 0) AS growth_pct
FROM yearly
ORDER BY growth_pct DESC
watch: The CASE WHEN pivot puts both years on one row, so growth is a plain subtraction.
Without the date filter, the 2011 and 2014 orders are summed into no column but still cost you time to explain.

metrics: Sum of SubTotal per territory and year.

viz_specs.title: Europe and Australia grew fastest, two US territories shrank
viz_specs.sub: Revenue growth 2013 vs 2012 by territory.
viz_specs.why: One value per category, ranked: bars from a zero line, so shrinking territories point down.

viz_specs.title: In dollars the gains are close
viz_specs.sub: Revenue added in 2013 vs 2012, $M.
viz_specs.why: The same ranking in dollars shows which gains are big and which come from a small base.

model: Germany grew fastest in percent (+366%), followed by France (+144%), the United Kingdom (+130%) and Australia (+99%).
Germany started from $0.55M, so its gain of $2.02M is similar to the other three. In dollars France added the most (+$2.25M). Northeast (-9%) and Southeast (-19%) shrank, and Central was flat.

Set the Europe and Australia targets from their dollar gains instead of their percentages, and ask the Northeast and Southeast teams what changed. One caveat: this is two years, and fast growth in a small market does not carry forward by itself.
checks: I compared full years only.
I looked at percent and dollars together.
I named the territories that shrank.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Online has most of the orders. Who brings the money?

brief.subject: Is online the main channel yet?
body: The dashboard shows far more online orders than sales-rep orders, and the online team wants more budget. Before I answer, I want to see both channels on orders and on revenue.
Please also show how the split changed from year to year.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which channel brings the revenue, why order counts mislead, and what to do about the budget.
facts: OnlineOrderFlag in ADW_Sales_orders: 1 = online, 0 = sales rep.
One row per order. Revenue = SubTotal.

questions: What share of orders is online, and what share of revenue?
How large is the average order in each channel?
Is the split changing from year to year?

frame.nudge: If one channel has 90% of the orders, does it have 90% of the revenue? What number links the two?
hyp: Online wins on order count but sales reps win on revenue.
Online's share of revenue is growing.
traps: A flag of 0 and 1 is unreadable in a report: label it with CASE WHEN.
Compare shares of the whole, not raw counts.
2011 starts in May and 2014 ends in June, so judge the yearly trend by shares, not by totals.

tables: Everything is on the order header: flag, date and subtotal.
Line level; not needed for channel totals.
Territories are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. COUNT(*) is orders, SUM(SubTotal) is revenue.
No join is needed. The whole answer comes from one table.
data.goal: One row per channel: orders, % of orders, revenue, % of revenue, average order value.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE ____ END AS channel
     , COUNT(*) AS orders
     , ...                      -- % of all orders: use SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER ()
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                      -- % of all revenue
     , ...                      -- average order value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE ____ END
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END AS channel
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)          AS pct_of_orders
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)                         AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(SubTotal) / SUM(SUM(SubTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0)                          AS avg_order_value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: The GROUP BY must repeat the CASE expression, not the alias, in SQL Server.
SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () is the grand total of the grouped counts. It does not need a second query.

extra_sql.title: The same split by year
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS online_m
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS sales_rep_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / SUM(SubTotal), 0) AS online_pct_of_revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year

viz_specs.title: Online is 88% of the orders and 27% of the revenue
viz_specs.sub: Share of orders and revenue by channel, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two shares per channel: grouped bars. The flip between the two bars is the whole message.

viz_specs.title: Sales reps lead in every year
viz_specs.sub: Revenue by channel and year, $M. 2011 starts in May and 2014 stops in June.
viz_specs.why: Two groups across four years: grouped bars, same colour per channel.

model: Sales reps bring the revenue: they write 12% of the orders but 73% of the revenue.

An average sales-rep order is worth $21,148, against $1,061 online, so 20 online orders equal one rep order. Online's share of revenue fell to 19% in 2012, then rose to 25% in 2013 and 42% in the first half of 2014, but sales reps led every year.

Do not move the budget on order counts. Keep the rep channel funded and ask the online team how they plan to raise the basket size. The data does not say whether the two channels serve the same kind of customer, so the comparison is a first look.
checks: I compared share of orders with share of revenue.
I used average order value to explain the gap.
I looked at the trend by year.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue grew in 2013: more customers or bigger orders?

brief.subject: What drove 2013, and is 2014 a decline?
body: Revenue in 2013 was about 30% above 2012, yet the average order looks smaller. I need to know where the growth came from: more customers, customers ordering more often, or bigger orders.
The dashboard also shows 2014 falling off a cliff. I present to the board next week and I don't want to explain a collapse that isn't real.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: the main driver, why order value fell, and what to say about 2014.
facts: Revenue is SubTotal in ADW_Sales_orders (before tax and freight).
That table has one row per order.

questions: Which of customers, orders per customer and order value moved most between 2012 and 2013?
Why did the average order value fall?
Is the 2014 drop real?

frame.nudge: Revenue is a product of simpler pieces. Which pieces can you measure, and can they move in opposite directions?
tree: Revenue = customers × orders per customer × average order value
Which piece moved most from 2012 to 2013
Whether each year in the data is complete
hyp: The customer count grew a lot.
Order value fell because the mix shifted toward smaller online orders.
traps: Check the date range before comparing years. A part-year looks like a decline.
Divide each total by the right count: customers for orders per customer, orders for order value.
An average can fall because the mix of orders changed, even if no single order got smaller.

tables: One row per order with date, customer, channel flag and value.
Line level; order totals already sit on the header.
Not needed for a company-wide view.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order, so COUNT(*) is orders and COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) is customers.
OnlineOrderFlag: 1 = online, 0 = sales rep.
data.goal: One row per year: orders, customers, orders per customer, average order value, revenue. Check the date range first.
data.skeleton:
-- Step 0: is every year complete?
SELECT MIN(OrderDate), MAX(OrderDate) FROM ADW_Sales_orders;

-- Step 1: the drivers by year
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , COUNT(*) AS orders
     , COUNT(DISTINCT ____) AS customers
     , ...        -- orders per customer
     , ...        -- average order value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
data.solution:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate)                                   AS order_year
     , COUNT(*)                                         AS orders
     , COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID)                       AS customers
     , ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID), 3) AS orders_per_customer
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0)               AS aov
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)              AS revenue_m
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year

pre.title: Step 0: date range
pre.sql: SELECT MIN(OrderDate) AS first_order, MAX(OrderDate) AS last_order FROM ADW_Sales_orders

watch: Orders per customer divides orders by distinct customers, not by rows.
2011 starts in May and 2014 ends in June. Compare full years only (2012 against 2013).

extra_sql.title: Index of 2013 vs 2012 (feeds the chart)
extra_sql.sql:
WITH y AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
         , COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID)                  AS customers
         , 1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS orders_per_customer
         , SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*)                    AS aov
         , SUM(SubTotal)                               AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
)
SELECT 'Customers' AS driver, ROUND(100.0 * b.customers / a.customers, 0) AS index_2012_100
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Orders per customer', ROUND(100.0 * b.orders_per_customer / a.orders_per_customer, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Average order value', ROUND(100.0 * b.aov / a.aov, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Revenue', ROUND(100.0 * b.revenue / a.revenue, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013

metrics: Distinct customers with at least one order in the year.
2013 value ÷ 2012 value × 100. Revenue is the product of the three drivers.

viz_specs.title: Customers drove the growth and order value fell
viz_specs.why: Four ratios against one baseline: bars with a reference line at 100.

dig.title: Why did order value fall? Split by channel
dig.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS online_share_of_orders_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS aov_online
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS aov_sales_rep
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year
dig.read: In 2013 online orders average about $853 and sales-rep orders about $20,582. Online went from 70% of orders in 2012 to 89% in 2013, so the average fell with the mix.

model: Customers drove the growth: in 2013 there were 3.5 times as many as in 2012, while the average order value fell to 36% of its 2012 level.
Revenue rose from $33.5M to $43.6M. Orders per customer barely moved (103% of 2012). Online orders, which are small (about $853), went from 70% to 89% of all orders and pulled the average down.

2014 is not a collapse. The data stops on 30 June 2014, so that year holds six months. Compare January to June 2014 with January to June 2013 before it goes to the board. This shows what changed, not why more customers arrived.
checks: I split revenue into customers × frequency × order value.
I checked the date range before comparing years.
I explained the lower average with mix.
I said what to do about 2014.

challenges.title: Do 10 customers carry the business?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles sells bikes, parts and clothing to shops (sales reps) and to people (online store).
context.situation: The finance team is writing the risk section of the annual plan. A board member heard that "a handful of big accounts pay the bills".
context.decision: Does the plan need a key-account protection program, or is revenue spread widely enough to skip it?

brief.subject: How dependent are we on our biggest customers?
body: The board wants one number for the risk section: how much of our revenue comes from our largest customers. If it is high I will ask for a key-account program. If it is low I will not.
Use all orders in the data and count revenue as order SubTotal. Show me the top 10, the next 90, the next 900 and everyone else, with how many customers sit in each group.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how concentrated is revenue, is it a risk, and what should Finance do.
facts: Customers are identified by CustomerID in ADW_Sales_orders.
The data covers May 2011 to June 2014.

questions: What share of revenue do the top 10 and the top 100 customers hold?
Who are the top 10: shops or online buyers?
Is that level of concentration a risk or a normal pattern?

frame.nudge: A share of revenue means little without a yardstick. Before you run anything, decide what share would worry you and what would not. What does the answer change?
tree: Share held by the top 10, top 100, top 1,000
Who the top customers are and how they buy
hyp: A few accounts hold a large part of revenue.
The biggest accounts are shops that order often.
traps: Ranking needs one row per customer first. Sum orders by CustomerID before you rank.
A big share for the top 1,000 is normal when there are 19,000 customers: compare the share of customers with the share of revenue.
Revenue by customer is not profit. Say so in your answer.

tables: One row per order: date, channel flag, customer, territory, SubTotal.
Order lines are not needed: SubTotal is already on the order.
Territory is not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. Add up SubTotal per customer first.
A window function (ROW_NUMBER) ranks the customers; a CASE WHEN turns the rank into a group.
data.goal: One row per customer group: customers, share of customers, revenue and share of revenue.
data.skeleton:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(SubTotal) AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY ____
),
r AS (
    SELECT revenue, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ____ DESC) AS rk
    FROM c
)
SELECT CASE WHEN rk <= 10 THEN '1. Top 10'
            WHEN ____ THEN '2. Next 90'
            ...
            ELSE '4. All others' END AS customer_group
     , COUNT(*) AS customers
     , ...                      -- share of customers, revenue, share of revenue
FROM r
GROUP BY ____
data.solution:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(SubTotal) AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
r AS (
    SELECT revenue, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rk
    FROM c
)
SELECT CASE WHEN rk <= 10   THEN '1. Top 10'
            WHEN rk <= 100  THEN '2. Next 90'
            WHEN rk <= 1000 THEN '3. Next 900'
            ELSE '4. All others' END AS customer_group
     , COUNT(*)                                                 AS customers
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)       AS pct_of_customers
     , ROUND(SUM(revenue), 0)                                   AS revenue
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(revenue) / SUM(SUM(revenue)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
FROM r
GROUP BY CASE WHEN rk <= 10   THEN '1. Top 10'
              WHEN rk <= 100  THEN '2. Next 90'
              WHEN rk <= 1000 THEN '3. Next 900'
              ELSE '4. All others' END
ORDER BY customer_group
watch: If you rank orders instead of customers, one customer with 12 orders fills 12 places.
SUM(SUM(revenue)) OVER () works because the window runs after the GROUP BY. A plain SUM(revenue) OVER () would not.

extra_sql.title: Who are the top 10? (customer, orders, revenue, whether they bought online)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT TOP 10 CustomerID
     , COUNT(*)                  AS orders
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal), 0)   AS revenue
     , MAX(OnlineOrderFlag)      AS bought_online
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CustomerID
ORDER BY revenue DESC

metrics: Share of revenue held by the top N customers.
Customers in the group ÷ all customers. Compare it with revenue share.
Revenue ÷ customers in the group. Shows how far apart the groups are.

viz_specs.title: Top 100 customers: half a percent of customers, 42% of revenue
viz_specs.sub: Share of customers and share of revenue by customer group, all orders.
viz_specs.why: Two shares across the same groups: paired bars show where revenue is out of proportion to headcount.

model: Not at the very top. The top 10 customers hold only 7.2% of revenue, so losing one would not hurt much. The concentration starts further down, in the top 100.

The top 10 hold 7.2% and the top 100 hold 42.3%. The top 1,000 customers (5.3% of customers) hold 76.6% of revenue, which is a normal long-tail shape. All ten top customers bought through sales reps: they placed 116 orders between them.

No key-account program is needed for a single customer. Finance should watch the top 100 reseller accounts as a group, since they carry about two fifths of revenue, and add margin by customer before deciding on any program. This is revenue, not profit.
checks: I answered the board's question first.
I ranked customers, not orders.
I compared share of revenue with share of customers.
I said what the numbers do not show (profit, trend).

challenges.title: Special offers: which discounts cost the most?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles sells bikes and parts to shops (sales reps) and to people (online). Reseller customers get special offers: volume discounts, clearance sales, new-product promotions.
context.situation: The commercial team renews the offer calendar every year. Nobody has added up what the offers cost.
context.decision: Which kinds of offer should stay on the calendar and which should be cut or re-priced?

brief.subject: What do our special offers really cost us?
body: Every year we renew about a dozen special offers. They look generous, and nobody has checked what they cost. I want to renew the ones that earn their keep and drop the rest.

For each offer type give me how many order lines it touched, the list value, what we invoiced, the discount we gave away, and the discount as a percent of list value. Offer 1 is "No Discount": leave it out of the table, but tell me how big discounted business is next to everything else.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how big are offers, which type costs the most, and what you would renew.
facts: List value = OrderQty × UnitPrice. Invoiced = LineTotal (already net of discount).
SpecialOfferID = 1 means no discount.

questions: How much of revenue sits on discounted lines?
How much discount did we give away, and in which offer type?
Which offer type is deepest relative to what it sells?

frame.nudge: A big offer in dollars and a deep offer in percent are different things. Which one answers Daniel's question, and what would you want next to it?
tree: Size of discounted business next to all business
Discount given in dollars, by offer type
Discount depth in percent of list value
hyp: A few offer types account for most of the discount given.
Clearance offers are the deepest.
traps: LineTotal is already after discount. Compute list value from quantity and price.
Leave offer 1 (no discount) out of the discount table, or every average gets diluted.
Discount given tells you the cost, not whether the offer created extra sales.

tables: One row per order line: quantity, list price, discount, LineTotal, special offer.
Describes each offer: type, discount percent, product scope.
Order date and channel are not needed for this cut.
Product detail is not needed at offer-type level.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders_detail: one row per order line, with SpecialOfferID.
ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer: one row per offer. The JOIN is many lines to one offer, so lines are not duplicated.
data.goal: One row per offer type (excluding no discount): lines, list value, revenue, discount given and discount percent of list.
data.skeleton:
SELECT so.Type AS offer_type
     , COUNT(*) AS order_lines
     , ROUND(SUM(d.OrderQty * d.UnitPrice), 0) AS list_value
     , ...                          -- revenue, discount given
     , ...                          -- discount as % of list value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer so ON ____
WHERE ____                          -- leave out 'No Discount'
GROUP BY so.Type
ORDER BY ____ DESC
data.solution:
SELECT so.Type                                              AS offer_type
     , COUNT(*)                                             AS order_lines
     , ROUND(SUM(d.OrderQty * d.UnitPrice), 0)              AS list_value
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal), 0)                           AS revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(d.OrderQty * d.UnitPrice - d.LineTotal), 0) AS discount_given
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.OrderQty * d.UnitPrice - d.LineTotal) / SUM(d.OrderQty * d.UnitPrice), 1) AS discount_pct_of_list
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_SpecialOffer so ON so.SpecialOfferID = d.SpecialOfferID
WHERE so.SpecialOfferID > 1
GROUP BY so.Type
ORDER BY discount_given DESC
watch: Percent of list is discount ÷ list value, not discount ÷ revenue. Revenue is already the smaller number.
A type with few lines can look extreme in percent. Read the line count next to it.

extra_sql.title: How big are discounted lines next to the rest?
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN SpecialOfferID = 1 THEN 'No discount' ELSE 'Special offer' END AS line_type
     , COUNT(*)                                               AS order_lines
     , ROUND(SUM(LineTotal), 0)                               AS revenue
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(LineTotal) / SUM(SUM(LineTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail
GROUP BY CASE WHEN SpecialOfferID = 1 THEN 'No discount' ELSE 'Special offer' END
ORDER BY line_type DESC

metrics: Quantity × list unit price, before any discount.
Revenue on discounted lines ÷ all revenue.

viz_specs.title: New Product gave away the most: $224K
viz_specs.sub: Discount given by offer type, all orders, in thousands of dollars.
viz_specs.why: One value per category, ranked: simple bars from zero.

viz_specs.title: Discontinued Product is the deepest: 36% off list
viz_specs.sub: Discount given as a percent of list value, by offer type.
viz_specs.why: A second metric on the same categories. The ranking changes, which is the point.

model: Offers are a small part of revenue (6.8%) but they cost real money: about $528K of discount, 7% off list on discounted lines.
New Product gave away the most ($224K), while Discontinued Product is the deepest at 36% off list. Volume discounts touch the most lines at a shallow rate.
Renew volume discounts. Re-price the deep clearance and promotion offers or time-box them, and check whether those offers brought extra units: this data shows the cost, not the lift.
checks: I put the size of discounted business next to total revenue.
I computed list value from quantity and price.
I looked at dollars and percent, and said they rank differently.
I named what is missing (did the offer lift sales?).

challenges.title: Online orders peak in Q4. Is that the season or the growth?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles runs an online store next to its reseller business. Online orders are small baskets (about $1,000) and make up most of the order count.
context.situation: The online team is planning staffing and stock for the next year. Last year's Q4 looked huge, so a manager wants to "plan for a big Q4 every year".
context.decision: Is there a real Q4 peak we should staff for, and how big is it?

brief.subject: Plan for a big Q4 every year?
body: Online orders in the last three months of 2013 were more than six times the first three months. My manager says that is Christmas and wants us to hire seasonal staff in Q4 every year.
Before I sign a staffing plan I want to know how much of that jump is the season. Look at online orders only, for 2012 and 2013, by quarter.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: is there a Q4 peak, how big is the seasonal part, and what should Linh plan.
facts: Online orders have OnlineOrderFlag = 1 in ADW_Sales_orders.
Use order counts. Sales rep orders follow a different rhythm and are left out.

questions: How much bigger is Q4 than Q1 in 2013?
Was Q4 also bigger than Q1 in 2012?
If the two years disagree, what else changed during 2013?

frame.nudge: One year of data cannot separate season from growth. What do you need to compare, and what would a true seasonal pattern look like in a second year?
tree: The month-by-month shape of both years
hyp: Q4 is higher than Q1 in both years.
The 2013 jump is too big to be only a season.
traps: One year of growth looks like a season. Compare the same quarters across years.
Growth can come as a single step. Look at the months as well as the quarters.
A rise in order counts says nothing about basket size.

tables: One row per order: date, channel flag, customer, territory, SubTotal.
Order lines are not needed to count orders.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. COUNT(*) counts orders.
Build the quarter with CASE WHEN on MONTH(OrderDate), then pivot the two years with conditional SUM.
data.goal: One row per quarter: online orders in 2012 and in 2013.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 3 THEN 'Q1'
            WHEN ____ THEN 'Q2'
            ...
            ELSE 'Q4' END AS quarter
     , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(OrderDate) = 2012 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_2012
     , ...                         -- 2013
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE ____                         -- online only, 2012 and 2013
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY quarter
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 3  THEN 'Q1'
            WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 6  THEN 'Q2'
            WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 9  THEN 'Q3'
            ELSE 'Q4' END AS quarter
     , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(OrderDate) = 2012 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_2012
     , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_2013
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE OnlineOrderFlag = 1
  AND YEAR(OrderDate) IN (2012, 2013)
GROUP BY CASE WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 3  THEN 'Q1'
              WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 6  THEN 'Q2'
              WHEN MONTH(OrderDate) <= 9  THEN 'Q3'
              ELSE 'Q4' END
ORDER BY quarter
watch: T-SQL does not let GROUP BY use the SELECT alias, so repeat the CASE.
Q4 in 2013 versus Q1 in 2013 mixes season with a year of growth. The 2012 comparison is the yardstick.

extra_sql.title: Month by month (feeds the line chart)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT MONTH(OrderDate) AS month_no
     , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(OrderDate) = 2012 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_2012
     , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_2013
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE OnlineOrderFlag = 1
  AND YEAR(OrderDate) IN (2012, 2013)
GROUP BY MONTH(OrderDate)
ORDER BY month_no

metrics: Q4 orders ÷ Q1 orders − 1, same year.
A month or quarter as a share of the same year's average. Only meaningful when the year is flat.
A sudden, lasting jump in level. A season goes up and comes back down.

viz_specs.title: Q4 beat Q1 by 30% in 2012 and 566% in 2013
viz_specs.sub: Online orders, Q4 compared with Q1 of the same year.
viz_specs.why: Two values compared: bars from zero. The gap between them is the message.

viz_specs.title: 2013 climbs in steps: June and July break the pattern
viz_specs.sub: Online orders per month. Months are drawn in the same order for both years.
viz_specs.why: Change over time, two series: lines show where the 2013 path leaves the 2012 path.

model: There is a small seasonal lift, about 30%, but most of the 2013 Q4 jump is growth, not the season. Plan for a modest Q4 peak, not a sixfold one.

In 2013 online orders rose from 852 in Q1 to 5,674 in Q4 (+566%). In 2012 the same two quarters were 594 and 771 (+30%). The 2013 line sits between 251 and 333 orders a month until May, then climbs: 533 in June and 1,564 in July, about 1,757 a month for the rest of the year. The level held in the first half of 2014 (about 1,855 a month).

Staff for the new level, which has held for a year, and add a seasonal buffer of roughly one third for Q4. Ask marketing what changed in mid-2013, and re-run this when 2014 has a full year. Caveat: two years give one seasonal observation, not a pattern.
checks: I compared the same quarters across two years.
I separated the seasonal part from the step in the level.
I gave the staffing call with a size.
I said what two years cannot prove.

challenges.title: 2013 revenue: new customers or returning ones?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles spends on two things: finding new customers and keeping existing ones. The marketing budget is split between them.
context.situation: 2013 was the best year so far. The CMO wants to move budget from retention to acquisition because "most of our customers are new".
context.decision: Where did 2013 revenue come from, and does that support moving budget to acquisition?

brief.subject: Where did 2013 revenue come from?
body: Most of the customers who ordered in 2013 had never ordered before. I want to shift budget from retention to acquisition, and I want to check the revenue before I do.
Split 2013 into new customers (first order ever in 2013) and returning customers (first order before 2013). Give me customers, orders, revenue, revenue per customer and share of revenue for each.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which group earns more, what the per-customer numbers say, and what that means for the budget.
facts: A customer's first order is the earliest OrderDate across all years.
Revenue is order SubTotal.

questions: How many customers and how much revenue does each group have?
What does one customer in each group bring?
Is the split the same in both channels?

frame.nudge: Counts of customers and dollars of revenue point in different directions here. Which one should drive a budget decision, and what makes the comparison fair?
tree: Customers, orders and revenue by type
Whether the channel mix hides the pattern
hyp: New customers are the majority by count.
Returning customers earn more per head.
traps: Find the first order over all years. If you only look at 2013, everyone looks new.
A new customer can order several times inside 2013. They are still new.
Compare per-customer numbers before comparing totals.

tables: One row per order: date, channel flag, customer, territory, SubTotal.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. Use it twice: once for each customer's first date, once for 2013 revenue.
A CTE (first_order) holds one row per customer. Joining back to orders does not duplicate customers.
data.goal: One row per customer type: customers, orders, revenue, revenue per customer and share of revenue.
data.skeleton:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, MIN(OrderDate) AS first_date
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY ____
)
SELECT CASE WHEN YEAR(f.first_date) = ____ THEN 'New in 2013' ELSE 'Returning' END AS customer_type
     , COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) AS customers
     , ...                         -- orders, revenue, revenue per customer, share
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
JOIN first_order f ON ____
WHERE YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2013
GROUP BY ____
data.solution:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, MIN(OrderDate) AS first_date
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CASE WHEN YEAR(f.first_date) = 2013 THEN 'New in 2013' ELSE 'Returning' END AS customer_type
     , COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID)                                  AS customers
     , COUNT(*)                                                      AS orders
     , ROUND(SUM(o.SubTotal), 0)                                     AS revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(o.SubTotal) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID), 0)      AS revenue_per_customer
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(o.SubTotal) / SUM(SUM(o.SubTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
JOIN first_order f ON f.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
WHERE YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2013
GROUP BY CASE WHEN YEAR(f.first_date) = 2013 THEN 'New in 2013' ELSE 'Returning' END
ORDER BY customer_type DESC
watch: Putting WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 inside the CTE changes every customer's first date.
COUNT(*) counts orders, COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) counts customers.

extra_sql.title: Does the pattern hold in both channels?
extra_sql.sql:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, MIN(OrderDate) AS first_date
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CASE WHEN YEAR(f.first_date) = 2013 THEN 'New in 2013' ELSE 'Returning' END AS customer_type
     , CASE WHEN o.OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END           AS channel
     , COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID)                                                 AS customers
     , ROUND(SUM(o.SubTotal), 0)                                                    AS revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
JOIN first_order f ON f.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
WHERE YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2013
GROUP BY CASE WHEN YEAR(f.first_date) = 2013 THEN 'New in 2013' ELSE 'Returning' END
       , CASE WHEN o.OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END
ORDER BY customer_type DESC, channel

metrics: First order ever falls in the year.
First order before the year, at least one order in the year.

viz_specs.title: Four in five customers are new, but returning customers bring more revenue
viz_specs.sub: Customers in thousands and revenue in $M, 2013 orders.
viz_specs.why: Same two groups on two measures: paired bars show the mismatch.

viz_specs.title: A returning customer brings 6.2x the revenue of a new one
viz_specs.sub: 2013 revenue per customer, by customer type.
viz_specs.why: One value per group: bars from zero, ranked.

model: Returning customers earned more: 63% of 2013 revenue from 21% of the customers. The data does not support moving budget away from retention on customer counts alone.

New customers are the majority (8,730 against 2,365) and brought $16.3M. Returning customers brought $27.4M, or $11,564 each against $1,864. Sales reps account for $23.1M of the returning revenue and $9.8M of the new revenue, so shops drive the gap.

Keep retention spend for reseller accounts, and judge acquisition on online customers separately. Caveat: this compares groups, not budgets. We have no cost per customer, and a new online customer may become a returning one next year.
checks: I defined new and returning with the first order across all years.
I compared revenue per customer as well as totals.
I checked the channel split before concluding.
I said what a budget decision still needs (cost per customer).

challenges.title: Average order value fell 75%. Did customers spend less?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles sells through two channels with very different baskets: online (small) and sales reps (large, to shops).
context.situation: The monthly report shows average order value (AOV) in the first half of 2014 far below the first half of 2013. The headline in the deck says "customers are spending a lot less".
context.decision: Is spending per order really collapsing, or did something else change in the numbers?

brief.subject: AOV is down by three quarters. Real?
body: Average order value for January to June 2014 is a fraction of January to June 2013. The deck I received says customers are spending much less per order, and the pricing team wants to react.

I would rather understand it first. Compare the same six months of both years, by channel, with the share of orders each channel holds. Then tell me how much of the drop is spending and how much is something else.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how big is the real change in spending, what else moved, and what the deck headline should say.
facts: AOV = total SubTotal ÷ number of orders.
Compare January to June in both years. 2014 data ends on 30 June.

questions: What is overall AOV in January to June of each year?
What is AOV inside each channel?
How much of the drop disappears when the channel mix is held constant?

frame.nudge: An average over two very different groups moves when the groups change size, even if nobody changes behaviour. What would you check before blaming customers?
tree: Overall AOV, same months both years
Share of orders by channel in each year
hyp: AOV fell inside each channel, but by less than it fell overall.
The online channel grew its share of orders.
traps: Compare the same months. January to December 2013 against January to June 2014 is not like for like.
Do not average the two channel AOVs. Weight them by order share.
A mix effect is a change in who buys, not in how much each buyer spends.

tables: One row per order: date, channel flag, customer, territory, SubTotal.
Line detail not needed at order level.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. SubTotal / COUNT(*) gives AOV for a group.
Group by year and channel; SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY year) gives each channel's share of that year's orders.
data.goal: One row per year and channel: orders, share of that year's orders, AOV.
data.skeleton:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END AS channel
     , COUNT(*) AS orders
     , ...                          -- share of the year's orders (window)
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0) AS aov
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE ____                          -- January to June, 2013 and 2014
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY order_year, channel
data.solution:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END AS channel
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(OrderDate)), 1) AS pct_of_orders
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0)                               AS aov
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE MONTH(OrderDate) <= 6
  AND YEAR(OrderDate) IN (2013, 2014)
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate), CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END
ORDER BY order_year, channel
watch: MONTH(OrderDate) <= 6 keeps January to June for both years.
AOV is a ratio. Compute SUM / COUNT per group, never an average of averages.

extra_sql.title: Overall AOV, the number in the deck
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate)                    AS order_year
     , COUNT(*)                          AS orders
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0) AS aov
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
WHERE MONTH(OrderDate) <= 6
  AND YEAR(OrderDate) IN (2013, 2014)
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year

metrics: Total order value ÷ number of orders.
Share of orders in each channel.
Change in AOV caused by a change in channel shares, with in-channel AOV held fixed.
Change in AOV caused by a change inside the channels, with shares held fixed.

viz_specs.title: At 2013's mix, 2014 AOV would be $5,272, not $1,705
viz_specs.sub: AOV, January to June. The middle bar uses 2014 channel AOVs weighted by 2013 order shares.
viz_specs.why: Three scenarios of one metric: bars from zero, the middle bar isolates the mix effect.

viz_specs.title: AOV also fell inside both channels, online most, but the mix does most of the work
viz_specs.sub: AOV by channel, January to June.
viz_specs.why: Two periods per category: paired bars.

model: Only partly. Overall AOV fell 75%, but about 70% of that drop is a change in who buys: the online channel took a much bigger share of orders.

Online orders grew from 74.6% to 94.6% of orders. Inside channels AOV fell 56% online and 15% with sales reps. At the 2013 mix, 2014 AOV would be $5,272: the rate effect is -$1,542 and the mix effect is -$3,567.

Change the headline to "online orders now make up 95% of orders; AOV fell 56% online and 15% with sales reps". Report AOV by channel from now on, and ask pricing and product what changed in the online basket, since online AOV is where the real decline sits. Caveat: January to June is one half-year, and online AOV may still be settling.
checks: I compared the same months in both years.
I separated the mix effect from the in-channel change.
I wrote a headline that does not blame customers for a mix shift.
I recommended reporting AOV by channel.

challenges.title: Which lapsed customers are worth a call?

context.company: AdventureWorks Cycles has 19,119 customers. Many shops order several times a year. Account managers have time to contact a few hundred of them.
context.situation: The account team wants a win-back list: customers who have gone quiet and who are worth the effort. "Lapsed" has no agreed definition yet.
context.decision: Who goes on the list, and does the cut-off that defines 'lapsed' make sense for how these customers actually reorder?

brief.from_: Sana Iqbal, Head of Account Management
brief.subject: Who should my team call this quarter?
body: My team can call a few hundred customers before the end of the quarter. I want to spend that effort on customers who used to buy, stopped, and were worth something.

Today is 1 July 2014 in this data. Group customers by how long since their last order (active up to 90 days, cooling 91 to 365, lapsed over 365) and by how many orders they placed (1, 2, 3 or more). Give me customers, lifetime revenue and revenue per customer in every cell.
Then check the cut-offs: do customers who reorder usually come back within 90 days, or is 365 the better line?
brief.ask: Reply in four sentences: which cell is the target, how many customers and what value, how you checked the definition of lapsed, and the caveat.
facts: Days since last order = 1 July 2014 minus the latest OrderDate of the customer.
Lifetime revenue is the sum of SubTotal over all of a customer's orders.

questions: Which recency and frequency cells hold the most value?
Which cell is the best target for calls?
Do repeat customers usually reorder within 90 days or within a year?

frame.nudge: 'Lapsed' only means something against how long customers normally wait. Before you pick a cell, find out the normal gap between orders. What does that do to the list?
tree: Value of each recency x frequency cell
Normal gap between two orders of the same customer
Cells that stay after the gap check
hyp: Repeat buyers who went quiet carry the most value.
The 90-day line is too short for these customers.
traps: Recency needs a reference date. Use the day after the last order in the data, not today's date.
One-time customers can be large but are not 'lost': they never became regular.
A 'lapsed' flag with a made-up cut-off sends calls to people who are simply between orders.

tables: One row per order: date, channel flag, customer, territory, SubTotal.
Line detail is not needed for customer value.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. Build one row per customer in a CTE: last order date, order count, revenue.
The gap check uses LAG(OrderDate) over each customer's orders, so it works at order grain.
data.goal: One row per recency group and frequency group: customers, lifetime revenue, revenue per customer.
data.skeleton:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT CustomerID
         , DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS days_since_last
         , COUNT(*) AS orders
         , SUM(SubTotal) AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY ____
)
SELECT CASE WHEN days_since_last <= 90 THEN '1. Active (0-90 days)'
            WHEN ____ THEN '2. Cooling (91-365 days)'
            ELSE '3. Lapsed (366+ days)' END AS recency_group
     , CASE WHEN orders >= 3 THEN '3+ orders' ... END AS frequency_group
     , COUNT(*) AS customers
     , ...                          -- lifetime revenue, revenue per customer
FROM c
GROUP BY ____, ____
ORDER BY recency_group, frequency_group
data.solution:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT CustomerID
         , DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01') AS days_since_last
         , COUNT(*)                                    AS orders
         , SUM(SubTotal)                               AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CASE WHEN days_since_last <= 90  THEN '1. Active (0-90 days)'
            WHEN days_since_last <= 365 THEN '2. Cooling (91-365 days)'
            ELSE '3. Lapsed (366+ days)' END AS recency_group
     , CASE WHEN orders >= 3 THEN '3+ orders' WHEN orders = 2 THEN '2 orders' ELSE '1 order' END AS frequency_group
     , COUNT(*)                          AS customers
     , ROUND(SUM(revenue), 0)            AS lifetime_revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(revenue) / COUNT(*), 0) AS revenue_per_customer
FROM c
GROUP BY CASE WHEN days_since_last <= 90  THEN '1. Active (0-90 days)'
              WHEN days_since_last <= 365 THEN '2. Cooling (91-365 days)'
              ELSE '3. Lapsed (366+ days)' END
       , CASE WHEN orders >= 3 THEN '3+ orders' WHEN orders = 2 THEN '2 orders' ELSE '1 order' END
ORDER BY recency_group, frequency_group
watch: Repeat the CASE expressions in GROUP BY: T-SQL cannot group by the alias.
Make sure the reference date comes after the last order in the data, or recency can go negative.

extra_sql.title: How long do repeat customers wait between orders?
extra_sql.sql:
WITH g AS (
    SELECT CustomerID
         , DATEDIFF(day, LAG(OrderDate) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate), OrderDate) AS gap_days
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                     AS repeat_orders
     , ROUND(AVG(gap_days), 0)                                      AS avg_gap_days
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN gap_days <= 90  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_within_90_days
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN gap_days <= 365 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_within_365_days
FROM g
WHERE gap_days IS NOT NULL

metrics: Days between the customer's last order and the reference date.
Sum of SubTotal over all of the customer's orders.
Days between two consecutive orders of the same customer.

viz_specs.title: Cooling repeat customers carry the most value: $49.0M
viz_specs.sub: Lifetime revenue of customers with 3 or more orders, by recency group.
viz_specs.why: One value per group: bars from zero. The highlighted bar is the target.

viz_specs.title: A lapsed repeat customer is worth $105,027 each
viz_specs.sub: Revenue per customer, customers with 3 or more orders.
viz_specs.why: Per-head value shows where one call is worth most, a different ranking from the totals.

model: Start with repeat customers who are cooling or lapsed. Cooling customers with 3 or more orders are 1,068 people worth $49.0M; lapsed ones are 119 people worth $12.5M, or $105,027 each.

The gap check weakens both lines: the average gap between two orders of the same customer is 261 days, 72% of repeat orders arrive within a year and only 25% within 90 days. A 90-day line would call most normal customers quiet, and even the 365-day line catches about 28% of orders that were simply late.

Call the 119 lapsed customers with 3 or more orders first (highest value per head), then the largest cooling accounts, and keep the one-order customers off the list. Treat "lapsed" as a reason to call, not proof of loss. Caveat: lifetime revenue is not margin and a customer who ordered long ago may have left for good; test the call on a sample and measure the response.
checks: I used a reference date after the last order.
I checked the 'lapsed' line against real reorder gaps.
I looked at per-customer value as well as totals.
I named a first target group and a caveat.

challenges.title: Is the Central office really the weakest at closing deals?

brief.subject: Central says it is not the problem. Is it?
body: Three regional offices (Central, East and West) sell the same product line. At the last review a manager said Central closes fewer deals than the others and asked to move pipeline to East and West.
Before I move any accounts I need to know whether the gap in win rate is real. Count closed deals only: Won or Lost. Open deals have no outcome yet.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: is there a gap, how sure are you, and what should Sofia do.
facts: Win rate = Won ÷ (Won + Lost).
Each sales agent belongs to one regional office, in CRM_sales_teams.

questions: What is each office's win rate on closed deals?
How many deals sit behind each rate?
Is the gap bigger than the normal wobble of a rate?

frame.nudge: A small gap between three rates only matters if it is bigger than the wobble you would expect by chance. What do you need besides the rates themselves?
tree: Win rate per office on closed deals
Number of deals behind each rate
The size of the gap against the margin of error
hyp: Central's rate is the lowest, but only by a little.
A gap this small could be noise.
traps: Open deals (Prospecting, Engaging) are not outcomes. Leave them out.
A rate from a small group moves more than a rate from a large one, so read the deal counts.
A ranking of three close numbers is a weak basis for moving pipeline.

tables: One row per deal with its stage.
Maps each agent to a regional office.
Customer companies; not part of this question.
Product list; not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Filter to Won and Lost.
CRM_sales_teams: one row per agent, so the JOIN does not duplicate deals.
data.goal: One row per regional office: closed deals, won deals and win rate.
data.skeleton:
SELECT t.regional_office
     , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = ____ THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won
     , ...                          -- win rate %
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage IN (____)
GROUP BY t.regional_office
data.solution:
SELECT t.regional_office
     , COUNT(*)                                                       AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)          AS won
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS win_rate_pct
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
WHERE p.deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY t.regional_office
ORDER BY win_rate_pct
watch: Leaving open deals in the denominator pulls every office's rate down by a different amount.
After the WHERE, COUNT(*) counts closed deals only. Check that it equals Won + Lost.

metrics: Closed deals per office. It sets how far a rate can move by chance.
Best office rate − worst office rate, in percentage points.
About 2 × √(rate × (1 − rate) ÷ deals). If two whiskers overlap, the gap may be chance.

viz_specs.title: Three offices, one overlapping band
viz_specs.sub: Win rate on closed deals, with the margin of error as whiskers.
viz_specs.why: Points with whiskers need no zero baseline. Overlapping whiskers say the gap may be chance.

model: No. The three offices win at almost the same rate, so there is no case for moving pipeline away from Central.
On 6,711 closed deals the win rates are Central 62.6%, East 63.0%, West 63.9%. Best and worst differ by 1.4 points, and each rate can move by about 2 points by chance, so the whiskers overlap.
Leave the allocation as it is and look for the real driver in another cut, such as product or sector. This says the offices do not differ, not that the win rate is good.
checks: I answered yes or no first.
I used closed deals only.
I compared the gap with the margin of error.
I did not invent a story for a small gap.

challenges.title: Which manager leads on revenue, and is it the team or one agent?

brief.subject: Bonus review: revenue by manager
body: I'm preparing the manager bonus review. I have a ranking of the six managers by revenue and I want to check it before I use it.

Is the manager ranking driven by the team or by one person?

Revenue per agent, to compare teams of different size
The top agents and their share of the total

Without that agent the ranking looks different.

Divide by the number of agents who actually closed deals, not by the team list.

Agent to manager and regional office.
Customers are not part of this question.
Products are not part of this question.

     , COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent) AS agents
     , COUNT(*) AS won_deals
     , ...                          -- revenue in $M
     , ...                          -- revenue per agent
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage = ____
GROUP BY t.manager, t.regional_office

SELECT t.manager
     , t.regional_office
     , COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent)                               AS agents
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)                    AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent), 0) AS revenue_per_agent
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY t.manager, t.regional_office
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC

The teams table lists 35 agents, but only 30 closed deals. Counting from the pipeline gives the real team size.

extra_sql.title: Top five agents (RANK() OVER plus a share of the total; feeds the second chart)
extra_sql.sql:
WITH agent AS (
    SELECT p.sales_agent, t.manager
         , COUNT(*)           AS won_deals
         , SUM(p.close_value) AS revenue
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
    JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
    WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
    GROUP BY p.sales_agent, t.manager
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *
         , RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC)                 AS rnk

    FROM agent
)
SELECT rnk, sales_agent, manager, won_deals
     , ROUND(revenue / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , pct_of_total
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY rnk

metrics: Manager revenue ÷ agents who closed at least one deal.
Agent revenue ÷ revenue of all agents.

viz_specs.title: Melvin Marxen's team leads on revenue
viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by manager, $M.
viz_specs.why: One value per manager, ranked: bars from zero.

viz_specs.title: One agent closes more than twice the next
viz_specs.sub: Top five agents by won revenue, $M.
viz_specs.why: The same ranking one level down shows how far the first agent stands from the rest.

Darcel Schlecht closed $1.15M, 12% of all revenue and 2.4 times the next agent. Without Darcel, Melvin's team would have $1.10M, level with Dustin Brinkmann's $1.09M.

I looked below the manager level.
I quoted the share of the top agent.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue by product series: why does the join lose a product?

brief.subject: Revenue by product series
body: I want won revenue for each product series (GTX, MG and GTK) for the roadmap meeting. The series name is in the products table, and the deals are in the pipeline table.
A colleague already ran a join and sent me the numbers, but the total looks too low compared with the sales report. Please redo it and tell me what went wrong.

Series live in CRM_products (columns product, series, sales_price).

questions: How much won revenue does each series bring?
Does the revenue by series add up to the total of all won deals?
If not, which product is missing and why?

frame.nudge: After a join, compare the total with the total before it. If the two differ, which rows did the join drop?
tree: Total won revenue before the join
Total won revenue after the join
Which product names fail to match
hyp: One product name is spelled differently in the two tables.
The missing product is a big seller.
traps: An INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows without a warning. Always check the total.
Look for the unmatched value with a LEFT JOIN and IS NULL.
Fix the name in the query with REPLACE, or on the data side if you own the table.

tables: Deals with product, stage and value.
Agents are not part of this question.
Customers are not part of this question.

CRM_products: one row per product, so the join keeps one row per deal as long as the names match.

-- Step 1: which names fail to match?
SELECT p.product, COUNT(*) FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
LEFT JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = p.product
WHERE pr.product IS ____
GROUP BY p.product;

-- Step 2: join again with the name fixed
SELECT pr.series, SUM(p.close_value) AS revenue
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = REPLACE(p.product, ____, ____)
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY pr.series

SELECT pr.series
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)                    AS revenue_m

FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = REPLACE(p.product, 'GTXPro', 'GTX Pro')
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY pr.series

FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p

WHERE pr.product IS NULL

challenges.title: Which customer sector is worth targeting?

brief.subject: Which sector should the next campaign target?
body: We have budget for one sector-focused campaign. I'd like to pick the sector where we win the most revenue, and I'd like to know whether that comes from closing better or from having more deals.
Use closed deals (Won or Lost) and the account's sector.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which sector brings the most revenue, whether it closes better than the others, and what to target.
facts: The sector of each customer is on CRM_Accounts, linked by the account name.
The data spells one sector technolgy. Keep the spelling when you filter.

questions: Which sector brings the most won revenue?
Does any sector have a clearly higher win rate?
Is a sector's revenue driven by deal count or by deal size?

frame.nudge: Revenue in a sector is deals × win rate × deal size. Which of the three actually differs between sectors?
tree: Deals and average deal size per sector
hyp: Win rates are similar, so revenue follows the number of deals.
A small sector may have a high average deal size.
traps: Use closed deals for the win rate, and Won deals for revenue and deal size.
Open deals have no account in many rows, so the inner join drops them. Closed deals all have one.
Do not read a 1 or 2 point gap in win rate as a strength.

tables: Deals with account, stage and value.
Agents are not part of this question.
Products are not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal.
CRM_Accounts: one row per account, so the join does not duplicate deals.
data.goal: One row per sector: closed deals, win rate, won revenue and average won deal size.
data.skeleton:
SELECT a.sector
     , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
     , ...                          -- win rate %
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                          -- average won deal size
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_Accounts a ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage IN (____)
GROUP BY a.sector
data.solution:
SELECT a.sector
     , COUNT(*)                                                                  AS closed_deals
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS win_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0)         AS avg_won_deal
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_Accounts a ON a.account = p.account
WHERE p.deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY a.sector
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC

Lost deals have a close_value of 0, so summing them in does no harm, but dividing by them does.

viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by customer sector, $M.

challenges.title: Who are the weakest closers, and can we tell?

context.company: A B2B company sells a range of computer hardware products to business accounts through a sales team of about 30 agents in three regional offices.
context.situation: The sales director wants to put the bottom five agents on a coaching plan. The ranking comes straight from a win-rate table.
context.decision: Which agents, if any, perform differently from the team, and who deserves coaching?

brief.subject: Bottom five on win rate: coaching plan?
body: Each agent has a different number of closed deals, and I know a rate from 120 deals is shakier than one from 550. I still need a list for the coaching plan.
For every agent give me closed deals, win rate, and the margin of error around the team's rate for that many deals. Flag the agents whose rate is farther from the team average than that margin.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how many agents really differ, who they are, and what you would do about the rest.
facts: Win rate = Won ÷ (Won + Lost). Open deals do not count.
Margin of error for a team rate p and n deals is about 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n).

questions: What are the win rate and the number of closed deals for each agent?
How wide is the margin of error for each agent?
How many agents differ from the team by more than that margin?

frame.nudge: Out of 30 agents, a few will sit at the bottom of any ranking. What would the ranking look like if every agent were exactly equal and only luck varied?
tree: Win rate and deals per agent
Margin of error for each agent's deal count
hyp: Some agents are below the team rate by more than chance allows.
Most of the bottom five are within chance.
traps: Open deals do not belong in the denominator.
A short list of 'bottom five' always exists, even when nobody is different.
A flag at 95% will catch about 1 in 20 agents by luck alone. Say so.

tables: One row per deal with its agent and stage.
Maps agents to offices; the question is per agent.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Filter to Won and Lost, group by sales_agent.
A second CTE holds the team rate once; a CROSS JOIN puts it next to every agent.
data.goal: One row per agent: closed deals, win rate, margin of error in points and a verdict.
data.skeleton:
WITH a AS (
    SELECT sales_agent
         , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = ____ THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE ____
    GROUP BY ____
),
t AS (SELECT 1.0 * SUM(won) / SUM(closed_deals) AS team_rate FROM a)
SELECT a.sales_agent, a.closed_deals
     , ...                          -- win rate %, margin of error
     , CASE WHEN ABS(agent rate - team_rate) > margin THEN 'Different from team' ELSE 'Within noise' END AS verdict
FROM a CROSS JOIN t
ORDER BY win_rate_pct, a.sales_agent
data.solution:
WITH a AS (
    SELECT sales_agent
         , COUNT(*)                                              AS closed_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS won
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
    GROUP BY sales_agent
),
t AS (
    SELECT 1.0 * SUM(won) / SUM(closed_deals) AS team_rate
    FROM a
)
SELECT a.sales_agent
     , a.closed_deals
     , ROUND(100.0 * a.won / a.closed_deals, 1)                                   AS win_rate_pct
     , ROUND(196 * SQRT(t.team_rate * (1 - t.team_rate) / a.closed_deals), 1)     AS margin_pts
     , CASE WHEN ABS(1.0 * a.won / a.closed_deals - t.team_rate)
                 > 1.96 * SQRT(t.team_rate * (1 - t.team_rate) / a.closed_deals)
            THEN 'Different from team' ELSE 'Within noise' END                    AS verdict
FROM a
CROSS JOIN t
ORDER BY win_rate_pct, a.sales_agent
watch: Dividing integers drops decimals: write 1.0 * won / closed.
The margin uses the team rate and the agent's own deal count, so small agents get wider bands.

metrics: Won ÷ closed deals across all agents (63.2%).
About 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n) for the team rate p and the agent's deals n.
Agent rate is outside the team rate ± margin.

viz_specs.title: Bottom five and top five agents, with the margin of error
viz_specs.sub: Win rate on closed deals, with whiskers for chance.
viz_specs.why: Points with whiskers need no zero baseline. A whisker that crosses the team line means the agent may be average.

model: Only 2 of 30 agents differ from the team beyond chance, so a bottom-five coaching plan would mostly coach luck.

The team wins 63.2% of closed deals. Rates run from 55.0% (Lajuana Vencill, 231 deals) to 70.4% (Hayden Neloms, 152 deals). Flagged: Lajuana Vencill (55.0%), Maureen Marcano (70.0%). 5 agents have fewer than 150 closed deals, and their margins are 8 points or more.

Coach the flagged agents only, review their deals for a pattern, and recheck after another quarter of data. For everyone else, avoid ranking people on rates from small samples. Caveat: with 30 agents and a 95% line, one flag may appear by chance.
checks: I used closed deals only.
I put a margin of error next to every rate.
I counted how many agents are really different instead of only naming who is last.
I said that one flag in thirty can be luck.

challenges.title: The open pipeline: which deals are stuck?

context.company: A B2B company sells a range of computer hardware products to business accounts through a sales team of about 30 agents in three regional offices.
context.situation: The quarter ends on 31 December. The forecast adds up every open deal, and the sales director suspects it includes deals that nobody is working.
context.decision: How many open deals should be questioned, and how much of the forecast depends on them?

brief.subject: Clean up the pipeline before the forecast
body: There are 1,589 deals in the Engaging stage, plus 500 in Prospecting that have no engage date yet. Before I forecast, I want to know how many Engaging deals are old.

Take 31 December 2017 as today. Group Engaging deals by days since they were engaged: 0 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90, 91 to 138 and over 138. Then tell me what a normal deal looked like when it closed, so I can judge what 'old' means.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how many deals look stuck, what you compared them with, and what I should do before the forecast.
facts: Age = days from engage_date to 31 December 2017.
138 days is the longest time any closed deal took, so deals older than that are outliers by this data's own history.

questions: How old are the Engaging deals?
How long did closed deals normally take?
How many open deals are older than any deal that ever closed?

frame.nudge: 'Old' only means something next to how long deals normally take. Where would you get that yardstick, and does it come from the open deals or the closed ones?
tree: Cycle time of closed deals (Won and Lost)
Deals older than the longest closed cycle
hyp: Most open deals are recent.
A tail of old deals inflates the forecast.
traps: Open deals have no close date. Age comes from today minus the engage date.
Prospecting deals have no engage date: leave them out of the age table and mention them.
The reference date matters: pick one and state it.

tables: Deal stage, engage date and close date.
Per-agent view is a follow-up, not this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Keep deal_stage = 'Engaging' for the open ones.
Closed deals (Won or Lost) have both dates, so their cycle is DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date).
data.goal: One row per age bucket: open deals and share of open deals.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 30 THEN '1. 0 to 30 days'
            WHEN ____ THEN '2. 31 to 60 days'
            ...
            ELSE '5. Over 138 days' END AS deal_age
     , COUNT(*) AS open_deals
     , ...                          -- share of open deals
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE ____
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY deal_age
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 30  THEN '1. 0 to 30 days'
            WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 60  THEN '2. 31 to 60 days'
            WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 90  THEN '3. 61 to 90 days'
            WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 138 THEN '4. 91 to 138 days'
            ELSE '5. Over 138 days' END AS deal_age
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS open_deals
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_open
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage = 'Engaging'
GROUP BY CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 30  THEN '1. 0 to 30 days'
              WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 60  THEN '2. 31 to 60 days'
              WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 90  THEN '3. 61 to 90 days'
              WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, '2017-12-31') <= 138 THEN '4. 91 to 138 days'
              ELSE '5. Over 138 days' END
ORDER BY deal_age
watch: Repeat the whole CASE in GROUP BY (no alias there in T-SQL).
The reference date is an assumption. State it next to the numbers.

extra_sql.title: What closed deals looked like (the yardstick)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                                  AS closed_deals
     , MAX(DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date))                                AS longest_cycle_days
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) <= 60  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_closed_within_60
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) <= 90  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_closed_within_90
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) <= 138 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_closed_within_138
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')

metrics: Days between engage date and the reference date (31 Dec 2017).
Days between engage date and close date for a closed deal.
Open deal older than the longest closed cycle in the data.

viz_specs.title: 1,291 Engaging deals are older than any deal that ever closed
viz_specs.sub: Engaging deals by days since engaged, as of 31 December 2017.
viz_specs.why: Ordered buckets, one value each: bars from zero. The last bar is the finding.

model: 1,291 of 1,589 Engaging deals (81%) are older than the longest deal that ever closed, so they should not count in the forecast until someone confirms them.

Closed deals took at most 138 days, 56% closed within 60 days and 80% within 90. Another 188 open deals sit between 91 and 138 days, where only about 20% of closed deals finished. The 500 Prospecting deals have no engage date and are not in this count.

Ask agents to confirm or close the over-138-day deals this week, cut the 91 to 138 day group to a probability that matches history, and report the forecast with and without them. Caveat: 31 December is our assumed 'today', and a deal can be slow for a good reason.
checks: I stated the reference date.
I compared deal age with the closed-deal history.
I did not count Prospecting deals as aged.
I told the VP what to do before the forecast.

challenges.title: Deals close better at quarter end. Real pressure or a reporting habit?

context.company: A B2B company sells a range of computer hardware products to business accounts through a sales team of about 30 agents in three regional offices.
context.situation: Sales leaders noticed that the win rate jumps in March, June, September and December. Quarterly targets and bonuses are paid on closed-won deals.
context.decision: Is the quarter-end jump a real selling effect we can use, or a sign that deals are being pulled or labelled to hit targets?

brief.subject: Why does the win rate spike at quarter end?
