body: The monthly win rate chart has a saw-tooth shape. Quarter-end months look much better than the months in between, and an exec asked if we should "just run more quarter-end pushes".

Give me win rate by month of close date (March to December, the months we have), flagged as quarter-end or not. Then compare the two groups, including how long won and lost deals took to close, and check whether every product shows the same pattern.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how big the effect is, what could explain it, and whether you would build a plan on it.
facts: Quarter-end months: March, June, September, December.
Closed deals only. The data has close dates from March to December 2017.

questions: What is the win rate in each month, and how many deals sit behind it?
How big is the gap between quarter-end months and the rest?
Does the pattern hold in every product, and is it a change in outcomes or in timing?

frame.nudge: A pattern tied to the calendar can be a real effect or a side effect of how deals are recorded. What data would separate the two explanations?
tree: Timing: do won and lost deals take different time at quarter end?
hyp: Quarter-end months win much more often.
The effect is the same in every product, which points to a process cause.
traps: Win rate by close month ignores deals still open. Say so.
A high win rate at quarter end can mean more wins or fewer recorded losses.
March has only part of its deals if the data starts in March: read the deal counts next to the rates.

tables: Stage, engage date, close date and value.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Filter to Won and Lost, group by the month of close_date.
Flag quarter-end months with CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (3, 6, 9, 12).
data.goal: One row per close month: type of month, closed deals, won deals and win rate.
data.skeleton:
SELECT MONTH(close_date) AS close_month
     , CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (____) THEN 'Quarter-end' ELSE 'Other' END AS month_type
     , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
     , ...                          -- won deals, win rate %
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE ____
GROUP BY ____, ____
ORDER BY close_month
data.solution:
SELECT MONTH(close_date)                                             AS close_month
     , CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (3, 6, 9, 12) THEN 'Quarter-end' ELSE 'Other' END AS month_type
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)         AS won
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS win_rate_pct
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY MONTH(close_date), CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (3, 6, 9, 12) THEN 'Quarter-end' ELSE 'Other' END
ORDER BY close_month
watch: Group by the month number, not the name, so months sort in calendar order.
A month with few deals gives a noisy rate: read the deal count beside it.

extra_sql.title: Quarter-end vs other months, with time to close
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (3, 6, 9, 12) THEN 'Quarter-end months' ELSE 'Other months' END AS month_type
     , COUNT(*)                                                                                   AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                        AS won
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1)           AS win_rate_pct
     , ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) END), 1) AS avg_days_won
     , ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Lost' THEN DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) END), 1) AS avg_days_lost
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY CASE WHEN MONTH(close_date) IN (3, 6, 9, 12) THEN 'Quarter-end months' ELSE 'Other months' END
ORDER BY month_type DESC

metrics: Win rate in quarter-end months − win rate in other months, in points.
A shift in when a deal is recorded, not whether it is won.

viz_specs.title: Win rate jumps in March, June, September and December
viz_specs.sub: Win rate on closed deals by close month, 2017.
viz_specs.why: Twelve ordered categories, one value each: bars from zero, with the quarter-end months highlighted.

model: The effect is large: 80.7% of closed deals are won in quarter-end months against 52.3% in the other months, a gap of 28 points. I would not build a selling plan on it yet.

The gap shows up in every product and in every quarter-end month, which points to a process or timing cause that affects all products. A typical quarter-end month has 519 won deals against 360 in other months, and only 124 lost deals against 329. Wins are pulled in and losses seem to be recorded later, so total closed deals per month barely change.

Check how the close date is set (is a lost deal closed when the customer says no, or when someone cleans the pipeline?) and compare the number of won deals per quarter, not per month. If wins per quarter stay flat, a quarter-end push only moves timing. Caveat: the data covers ten months of one year.
checks: I counted deals next to each rate.
I compared quarter-end months with the rest.
I checked whether the pattern holds in every product.
I offered a timing explanation next to the selling one.

challenges.title: How long does a sale take, and does it depend on the product?

context.company: A B2B company sells a range of computer hardware products to business accounts through a sales team of about 30 agents in three regional offices.
context.situation: Finance builds the cash forecast from won deals. They assume 'about two months' between first contact and a signed deal for every product.
context.decision: Is one number right for all products, and is the average the right way to describe how long a deal takes?

brief.subject: Sales cycle length by product
body: I use "60 days from engagement to close" in the cash forecast for every product. Sales says that is too long for some and too short for others.

For won deals, give me per product: number of deals, mean days, median days and the share closed within 60 days. Then compare won and lost deals overall, because I want to know if a quick 'no' is part of the story.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: what cycle length I should use, whether it differs by product, and what the mean hides.
facts: Cycle = days from engage_date to close_date.
The Lab's SQL has no MEDIAN function; sort the deals with ROW_NUMBER and take the middle one or two.

questions: What is the typical cycle for each product?
Is the difference between products bigger than a few days?
Do lost deals close faster or slower than won deals?

frame.nudge: A forecast needs a rule of thumb, but one number for seven products may hide structure, or may be fine. How would you tell the difference?
tree: Spread between fastest and slowest product
Share of deals within the assumed 60 days
hyp: Products differ by only a few days.
Won deals take longer than lost deals.
traps: Use won deals for the cash forecast. Lost deals never pay.
A product with 25 deals (GTK 500) has a very rough average.
Mean and median can differ when a few deals take very long.

tables: Stage, product, engage and close dates.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Won deals have both dates.
Median per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY cycle_days) and COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY product); the middle rows are where rn * 2 IN (n, n + 1, n + 2).
data.goal: One row per product: won deals, mean days, median days and share closed within 60 days.
data.skeleton:
WITH d AS (
    SELECT product
         , DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date) AS cycle_days
         , ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY ____) AS rn
         , COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY ____) AS n
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
)
SELECT product
     , COUNT(*) AS won_deals
     , ROUND(AVG(1.0 * cycle_days), 1) AS mean_days
     , ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN rn * 2 IN (n, n + 1, n + 2) THEN 1.0 * cycle_days END), 1) AS median_days
     , ...                          -- share within 60 days
FROM d
GROUP BY product
data.solution:
WITH d AS (
    SELECT product
         , DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date)                                   AS cycle_days
         , ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date)) AS rn
         , COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY product)                                     AS n
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
)
SELECT product
     , COUNT(*)                                                      AS won_deals
     , ROUND(AVG(1.0 * cycle_days), 1)                                     AS mean_days
     , ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN rn * 2 IN (n, n + 1, n + 2) THEN 1.0 * cycle_days END), 1) AS median_days
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN cycle_days <= 60 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_within_60_days
FROM d
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY median_days, product
watch: AVG on integers truncates: multiply by 1.0 first.
The median row is the middle one for odd n and the average of two middle rows for even n; the IN list covers both.

extra_sql.title: Won vs lost deals
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT deal_stage
     , COUNT(*)                                               AS deals
     , ROUND(AVG(1.0 * DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date)), 1) AS mean_days
     , MIN(DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date))            AS shortest
     , MAX(DATEDIFF(day, engage_date, close_date))            AS longest
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY deal_stage
ORDER BY deal_stage DESC

metrics: Days between engage date and close date.
The middle value of the sorted cycle times. Half the deals are faster.
Won deals closed in 60 days or fewer ÷ won deals.

viz_specs.title: Mean and median cycle: products sit within about 22 days of each other
viz_specs.sub: Days from engage to close, won deals, by product.
viz_specs.why: Two summaries of the same distribution: paired bars show where they agree and disagree.

model: Sixty days is a fair single assumption for the typical won deal: the median is 57 days and the mean 51.8. What it hides is the spread, since only 52% of won deals close within 60 days.

By median, GTXPro is fastest (47 days) and GTK 500 slowest (69 days, but only 15 deals); the larger products fall within 14 days of each other, so a separate assumption per product adds little. Lost deals are shorter: 41.5 days on average against 51.8 for won deals, so a quick 'no' is common.

Keep one timing curve for cash planning (for example 'half of won deals close within 57 days, and about 48 in 100 take longer than 60') and revisit GTK 500 when it has more deals. Caveat: cycle is measured on closed deals only; deals that are still open and slow are not in these averages.
checks: I used won deals for the cash forecast.
I compared mean with median.
I read the product differences against the number of deals.
I gave Finance a number they can use.

challenges.title: What is the open pipeline worth in dollars?

context.company: A B2B company sells a range of computer hardware products to business accounts through a sales team of about 30 agents in three regional offices.
context.situation: The CFO wants a revenue estimate from the open pipeline for the next period. Sales leaders usually answer with the sum of all open deals' list value, which is not what will close.
context.decision: What is a defensible dollar estimate of the open pipeline, and how wide is the range around it?

brief.subject: Pipeline-based revenue estimate
body: There are 2,089 open deals (500 Prospecting and 1,589 Engaging). Open deals have no value yet, so I need an estimate from history.

Per product, take the open deals, the historical win rate and the average value of a won deal, and multiply them: expected value = open deals × win rate × average won value. Then tell me how wide the range is and what could make the estimate wrong.
brief.ask: Reply in four sentences: the base estimate, the range, the product that matters most, and the biggest caveat.
facts: Win rate = Won ÷ (Won + Lost). Average won value = total close_value of won deals ÷ number of won deals.
Prospecting and Engaging are the two open stages.

questions: How many open deals, what win rate and what average won value does each product have?
What is the expected value by product and in total?
How much could the total move if the win rate and the average value are only estimates?

frame.nudge: An estimate with no range invites false precision. Which inputs are uncertain, and which product is most exposed to that uncertainty?
tree: Expected value and a range around it
hyp: The two largest products make up most of the expected value.
Small products with few closed deals carry a wide range.
traps: Open deals have no value: do not add up a field that is empty.
Win rate comes from closed deals. Prospecting deals are earlier than Engaging ones and likely win less, so the base is probably high.
Average won value is skewed by a few large deals (GTK 500). A range makes that visible.

tables: Product list prices are not used: use realised won values.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Build per-product counts with conditional SUM.
Expected value = open deals × win rate × average won value, per product, then summed.
data.goal: One row per product: open deals, win rate, average won value and expected value.
data.skeleton:
WITH h AS (
    SELECT product
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS closed_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN close_value ELSE 0 END) AS won_value
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage IN (____) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_deals
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    GROUP BY ____
)
SELECT product, open_deals
     , ...                          -- win rate %
     , ...                          -- average won value
     , ...                          -- expected value
FROM h
ORDER BY expected_value DESC
data.solution:
WITH h AS (
    SELECT product
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)       AS closed_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                  AS won_deals
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN close_value ELSE 0 END)        AS won_value
         , SUM(CASE WHEN deal_stage IN ('Prospecting', 'Engaging') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_deals
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
    GROUP BY product
)
SELECT product
     , open_deals
     , ROUND(100.0 * won_deals / closed_deals, 1)                              AS win_rate_pct
     , ROUND(1.0 * won_value / won_deals, 0)                                   AS avg_won_value
     , ROUND(open_deals * (1.0 * won_deals / closed_deals) * (1.0 * won_value / won_deals), 0) AS expected_value
FROM h
ORDER BY expected_value DESC
watch: Use 1.0 * to avoid integer division in the win rate and the average.
A product with 25 closed deals has a win rate you cannot rely on. Look at the range.

metrics: Open deals × win rate × average won value.
The estimate recomputed with the win rate and average value at the edges of their 95% intervals.
Prospecting deals are earlier and probably win less than the historical average.

viz_specs.title: GTXPro leads at $1,019K, and small products have wide ranges
viz_specs.sub: Expected value of the open pipeline by product, with a 95% range as whiskers.
viz_specs.why: A total per category with uncertainty: bars from zero, whiskers for the range.

model: The open pipeline is worth about $3.1M in expected value, with a range of $2.9M to $3.4M. Use the base for planning and the low end for commitments.

GTXPro and GTX Plus Pro make up 58% of the estimate. Win rates are close across products (around 63%), so value is driven by average deal size, which runs from $55 to $26,707. GTK 500 has the widest range relative to its estimate ($157K to $330K around $240K) because it rests on only 25 closed deals.

The biggest caveat is stage: 500 of the open deals are still Prospecting, which are earlier than Engaging deals. Every closed deal has an engage date, so the historical win rate describes deals that reached Engaging, and the base is likely too high. Report the estimate by stage once the data allows, and refresh the win rate each quarter.
checks: I did not add up empty or list values for open deals.
I gave a range as well as a point.
I named the product that drives the result.
I raised the stage caveat.

challenges.title: Which product categories earn the most profit?

brief.subject: Category profit for the range review
body: We review the product range twice a year and the last review used revenue only. This time I want profit as well, so we don't drop or push a category for the wrong reason.
Use all orders in the data. Revenue is quantity times the unit price in USD, and profit is quantity times (unit price − unit cost).
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which categories earn the profit, whether margins differ, and what that means for the review.
facts: GBE_Sales has one row per order line with the product key and the quantity.
Prices and costs are in USD on GBE_Products, which also holds the category.

questions: Which categories bring the most revenue and the most profit?
Do the margins differ much between categories?
What are the five most profitable subcategories?

frame.nudge: Revenue and profit can rank categories differently. What would make that happen, and how would you check it?
tree: Whether the profit ranking differs from the revenue ranking
hyp: Computers lead on both.
Margins are close across categories, so the two rankings match.
traps: Price and cost live on the product, quantity lives on the sale. Multiply them line by line before you sum.
Do not average the margin of single products. Divide total profit by total revenue.
Do not sum Unit_Price_USD alone: a line of 3 units earns 3 times the price.

tables: Order lines with product key and quantity.
Category, unit price and unit cost in USD.
Stores are not part of this question.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line. Quantity is on this row.
GBE_Products: one row per product, so the join keeps one row per order line.
data.goal: One row per category: revenue, profit and margin %. Then list the five most profitable subcategories.
data.skeleton:
SELECT p.Category
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                         -- profit in $M: quantity x (price - cost)
     , ...                         -- margin %
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON ____
GROUP BY p.Category
data.solution:
SELECT p.Category
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2)                          AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD)) / 1000000.0, 2)      AS profit_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD))
             / SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD), 1)                                   AS margin_pct
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY p.Category
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: The margin is profit divided by revenue at the category level, not an average of product margins.
Round only in the final SELECT. Rounding inside the sum changes the totals.

extra_sql.title: Top five subcategories by profit
extra_sql.sql:
WITH sub AS (
    SELECT p.Subcategory
         , SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD)) AS profit
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    GROUP BY p.Subcategory
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY profit DESC) AS rnk
    FROM sub
)
SELECT rnk, Subcategory, ROUND(profit / 1000000.0, 2) AS profit_m
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY rnk

metrics: Sum of quantity × (unit price − unit cost).

viz_specs.title: Computers and home appliances lead on revenue and profit
viz_specs.sub: Revenue and profit by category, $M, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two values per category in the same unit: grouped bars.

viz_specs.title: Margins are close in every category
viz_specs.sub: Profit as a percent of revenue, by category.
viz_specs.why: On a 0 to 100 scale, near-equal bars show that margin does not separate the categories.

model: Computers earn the most profit ($11.3M on $19.3M of revenue), followed by home appliances ($6.3M). Together they make 54% of all profit.

Margins are almost the same everywhere, from 55% (Games and Toys) to 61% (Music, Movies and Audio Books), so the profit ranking follows the revenue ranking. The most profitable subcategory is Desktops ($5.63M).

Judge the range by volume, since no category is a profit trap and none is a hidden winner. Games and toys are the smallest at $0.72M of revenue. This uses list prices and costs, so it ignores discounts and returns.
checks: I multiplied quantity by price and cost on each line.
I compared revenue rank with profit rank.
I computed margin from totals.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which country's stores earn the most per square meter?

brief.from_: Marcus Hale, Head of Retail Operations
brief.subject: Store space: where does it work hardest?
body: We are choosing where to put the next store budget. Total revenue by country favors the big markets, so I want revenue per square meter of store space.
Use 2019, the last full year before the drop in 2020. Count physical stores only (the online store has no floor space), and only stores that were open for the whole year.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which countries use their space best, which worst, and what to do with the budget.
facts: GBE_Stores has the country, the floor space (Square_Meters) and the open date of each store.
Online orders sit under StoreKey = 0. Exclude them.

questions: What is the revenue per square meter in each country?
Which stores should be left out so the comparison is fair?
How big is the gap between the best and the worst country?

frame.nudge: Revenue per square meter divides two things that live in different tables. At what level do you add each one up so that neither is counted twice?
tree: Both rolled up to country, then revenue ÷ space
hyp: The country with the most stores is not the one with the best revenue per square meter.
Small stores earn more per square meter.
traps: Add revenue up per store first. Joining sales to stores row by row repeats the floor space on every sale.
Stores that opened in 2019 had only part of a year. Leave them out.
Some stores sold nothing in 2019. They are not in the revenue table and drop out of the join.

tables: Order lines with the store key and the date.
Unit price to turn quantity into revenue.
Country, floor space and open date.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line, many per store. Sum to one row per store before you join to the stores table.
GBE_Stores: one row per store, so each store's floor space is counted once.
data.goal: One row per country: stores, floor space, 2019 revenue and revenue per square meter.
data.skeleton:
WITH store_rev AS (
    SELECT s.StoreKey, SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.StoreKey <> 0
      AND s.Order_Date >= ____ AND s.Order_Date < ____
    GROUP BY s.StoreKey
)
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*) AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters) AS square_meters
     , ...                       -- revenue per square meter
FROM GBE_Stores st
JOIN store_rev r ON ____
WHERE st.Open_Date < ____
GROUP BY st.Country
data.solution:
WITH store_rev AS (
    SELECT s.StoreKey
         , SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.StoreKey <> 0
      AND s.Order_Date >= '2019-01-01' AND s.Order_Date < '2020-01-01'
    GROUP BY s.StoreKey
)
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters)                             AS square_meters
     , ROUND(SUM(r.revenue) / 1000000.0, 2)              AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(r.revenue) / SUM(st.Square_Meters), 0)  AS usd_per_sqm
FROM GBE_Stores st
JOIN store_rev r ON r.StoreKey = st.StoreKey
WHERE st.Open_Date < '2019-01-01'
GROUP BY st.Country
ORDER BY usd_per_sqm DESC
watch: Joining sales rows straight to stores and then summing Square_Meters adds each store's space once per sale.
Revenue and floor space must cover the same stores, so both come from the joined rows.

extra_sql.title: For comparison: all stores per country, whether or not they sold in 2019
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*)                                       AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters)                          AS square_meters
FROM GBE_Stores st
WHERE st.StoreKey <> 0
GROUP BY st.Country
ORDER BY st.Country

metrics: Sum of quantity × unit price per store in 2019.
Country revenue ÷ country floor space, same stores in both.
Open before the year starts and with sales in the year.

viz_specs.title: US stores earn more than twice what Australian stores do per square meter
viz_specs.sub: 2019 revenue per square meter of floor space, USD, stores open all year.
viz_specs.why: One value per country, ranked: bars from zero.

model: The United States uses its space best at $242 per square meter in 2019, and Australia uses it worst at $104.

The gap is 2.3 times. Canada ($234) is close behind the US, then Italy ($181) and France ($164), while Germany ($125) and the Netherlands ($105) sit near the bottom. The US result comes from 20 comparable stores, so it is not one lucky shop.
Put the next budget into the US and look at Australia and the Netherlands before adding space there. Floor space is only one driver: store age, local prices and product mix are not in this data.
checks: I summed revenue per store before joining to the stores table.
I used comparable stores only.
I excluded the online store.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue fell in 2020. Did online hold up better than stores?

brief.subject: 2020 against 2019, by channel
body: Revenue dropped sharply in 2020. The board asks whether our online store cushioned the fall, because the plan for next year leans on it.
Compare each quarter of 2020 with the same quarter of 2019, for online and for stores separately.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how big the fall was, whether online did better, and what that means for the plan.
facts: Online orders have StoreKey = 0 in GBE_Sales. All other keys are physical stores.
Revenue = quantity × unit price (USD).

questions: How much did total revenue fall in 2020?
In which quarters did the fall happen, for online and for stores?
Did online fall less than the stores?

frame.nudge: Compare each 2020 quarter with the same quarter in 2019, not with the quarter before it. Why does that matter for retail data?
tree: Revenue per year, to size the fall and check the date range
2020 as a percent of 2019 for each quarter and channel
Online's share of revenue in each year
hyp: Online fell less than stores in the first months of the crisis.
The fall is large in both channels in the second half.
traps: Check the date range first. The last year in the data is a part-year.
Compare the same quarter of two years to remove seasonality.
Do not put 0 and 1 flags on a chart. Say online and stores.

tables: Order lines with date, store key and quantity.
Unit price to turn quantity into revenue.
Online is already identified by StoreKey = 0.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line.
GBE_Products: one row per product, so the join does not duplicate lines.
data.goal: One row per quarter: 2020 revenue as a percent of the same quarter in 2019, for online and for stores.
data.skeleton:
-- Step 0: size the year and check the dates
SELECT YEAR(s.Order_Date), ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2), MIN(s.Order_Date), MAX(s.Order_Date)
FROM GBE_Sales s JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY YEAR(s.Order_Date);

-- Step 1: one row per quarter, four sums (online/store x 2019/2020)
WITH q AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1' ... END AS quarter
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN ____ ELSE 0 END) AS online_2019
         , ...
    FROM ...
)
SELECT quarter, ...        -- 2020 as % of 2019 for each channel
FROM q
data.solution:
WITH q AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 6 THEN 'Q2'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 9 THEN 'Q3'
              ELSE 'Q4' END AS quarter
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS online_2019
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2020 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS online_2020
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey <> 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS store_2019
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey <> 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2020 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS store_2020
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.Order_Date >= '2019-01-01' AND s.Order_Date < '2021-01-01'
    GROUP BY CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 6 THEN 'Q2'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 9 THEN 'Q3'
              ELSE 'Q4' END
)
SELECT quarter
     , ROUND(100.0 * online_2020 / online_2019, 0) AS online_pct_of_2019
     , ROUND(100.0 * store_2020 / store_2019, 0)   AS store_pct_of_2019
     , ROUND((online_2020 + store_2020) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_2020_m
     , ROUND((online_2019 + store_2019) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_2019_m
FROM q
ORDER BY quarter

pre.title: Step 0: revenue per year and the date range
pre.sql:
SELECT YEAR(s.Order_Date) AS order_year
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , MIN(s.Order_Date) AS first_day
     , MAX(s.Order_Date) AS last_day
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY YEAR(s.Order_Date)
ORDER BY order_year

watch: T-SQL has no QUARTER() function. A CASE on MONTH() works in every dialect.
A pivot with CASE WHEN keeps both years on one row, so the percent is a plain division.

metrics: Revenue in a 2020 quarter ÷ revenue in the same 2019 quarter × 100.
Online revenue ÷ total revenue in the year.

viz_specs.title: Both channels fall away after the first quarter
viz_specs.sub: 2020 revenue as a percent of the same quarter in 2019.
viz_specs.why: Two channels across four quarters: two lines on the same scale.

model: Revenue fell 49% in 2020, from $18.3M to $9.3M, and online did not cushion it for long.
Q1 was level with 2019 in both channels. In Q2 online held up better (69% of 2019 against 56% for stores), but by Q3 online was at 30% and stores at 29%, and in Q4 at 22% and 20%.
Do not build next year's plan on online alone: it fell nearly as far as the stores. The data shows what dropped, not why, so ask Operations whether stock, delivery or demand caused it.
checks: I compared the same quarter across two years.
I split online from stores.
I checked the date range.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which age group should our campaign target?

context.company: Global Electronics Retailers sells phones, computers, audio and home appliances through stores and an online shop in several countries.
context.situation: Marketing has budget for one campaign aimed at a single age group. The CMO guesses it should be the oldest customers because "they are our biggest group".
context.decision: Which age group is worth targeting, and does age separate good customers from average ones at all?

brief.subject: One campaign, one age group
body: I can fund a single campaign next quarter. I need to pick the age group that gives the best return, and I would like to see the numbers first.

Use the customers who bought something. Work out each customer's age at the end of 2020 from the birth year, put them in six bands (under 25, 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54, 55 to 64, 65 and over) and give me customers, share of customers, revenue, share of revenue and revenue per customer for each band.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which band to target, what the numbers say about age, and what you would test instead.
facts: Revenue = Quantity × Unit_Price_USD, summed over all sales lines of the customer.
Birthday is text in the form m/d/yyyy: the last four characters are the year.

questions: How many customers and how much revenue does each age band hold?
Does revenue per customer differ by band?
If the big band is big only because it has more people, what should the CMO do?

frame.nudge: A share of revenue can be large only because the group is large. Which of these two numbers tells you the group is better, and which only tells you it is bigger?
tree: Revenue per customer next to the totals
Band width: unequal bands are not comparable by size
hyp: The oldest band holds the most revenue.
Revenue per customer is almost the same in every band.
traps: The 65+ band is open-ended and spans 20 years, while others span 10. Compare per customer.
Only customers who bought have revenue. Registered customers who never bought would drag averages to zero.
A flat result is still a result: it says age is not the lever.

tables: One row per sales line: customer, product, quantity.
Store is not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per line. First sum revenue per customer in a CTE, so each customer is one row.
RIGHT(Birthday, 4) is the birth year; age at end of 2020 is 2020 minus the year.
data.goal: One row per age band: customers, share of customers, revenue, share of revenue and revenue per customer.
data.skeleton:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT s.CustomerKey
         , 2020 - CAST(RIGHT(cu.Birthday, 4) AS INT) AS age
         , SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Customers cu ON ____
    JOIN GBE_Products p   ON ____
    GROUP BY s.CustomerKey, ____
)
SELECT CASE WHEN age < 25 THEN '1. Under 25'
            WHEN ____ THEN '2. 25-34'
            ...
            ELSE '6. 65 and over' END AS age_band
     , COUNT(*) AS customers
     , ...                          -- shares, revenue, revenue per customer
FROM c
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY age_band
data.solution:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT s.CustomerKey
         , 2020 - CAST(RIGHT(cu.Birthday, 4) AS INT)        AS age
         , SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD)               AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Customers cu ON cu.CustomerKey = s.CustomerKey
    JOIN GBE_Products p   ON p.ProductKey   = s.ProductKey
    GROUP BY s.CustomerKey, RIGHT(cu.Birthday, 4)
)
SELECT CASE WHEN age < 25 THEN '1. Under 25'
            WHEN age < 35 THEN '2. 25-34'
            WHEN age < 45 THEN '3. 35-44'
            WHEN age < 55 THEN '4. 45-54'
            WHEN age < 65 THEN '5. 55-64'
            ELSE '6. 65 and over' END AS age_band
     , COUNT(*)                                                      AS customers
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)            AS pct_of_customers
     , ROUND(SUM(revenue), 0)                                        AS revenue
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(revenue) / SUM(SUM(revenue)) OVER (), 1)    AS pct_of_revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(revenue) / COUNT(*), 0)                             AS revenue_per_customer
FROM c
GROUP BY CASE WHEN age < 25 THEN '1. Under 25'
              WHEN age < 35 THEN '2. 25-34'
              WHEN age < 45 THEN '3. 35-44'
              WHEN age < 55 THEN '4. 45-54'
              WHEN age < 65 THEN '5. 55-64'
              ELSE '6. 65 and over' END
ORDER BY age_band
watch: If you join sales to customers and group by band directly, customers with many lines are counted many times. Aggregate to one row per customer first.
RIGHT(Birthday, 4) is text. CAST it before doing arithmetic.

extra_sql.title: Who is in the data: registered customers vs customers who bought
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM GBE_Customers)                       AS registered_customers
     , COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerKey)                                    AS customers_who_bought
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerKey) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM GBE_Customers), 1) AS pct_who_bought
FROM GBE_Sales

metrics: Revenue of the band ÷ all revenue. Large when the band is large.
Revenue ÷ customers who bought, within the band.

viz_specs.title: The 65+ band holds 31% of revenue, and 31% of customers
viz_specs.sub: Share of customers and share of revenue by age band.
viz_specs.why: Two shares for each band: paired bars that track each other show that size explains revenue.

viz_specs.title: Revenue per customer is almost flat across age: $4,530 to $4,792
viz_specs.sub: Revenue per customer who bought, by age band.
viz_specs.why: One value per band against a reference line: a flat row of bars is the finding.

model: Age is not the lever here. The 65+ band holds the most revenue (31%) only because it holds the most customers (31%); a customer in any band brings about $4,690.

Revenue per customer ranges from $4,530 (45-54) to $4,792 (Under 25), a spread of 6%. The 65+ band is also open-ended (65 to 85), so it is wider than the others. Only 78% of the 15,266 registered customers have bought.

Do not pick a band on size. Test campaigns by product category, country or channel instead, and look at the registered customers who never bought as a separate target. Caveat: this describes who bought in the past, not who responds to a campaign.
checks: I aggregated to one row per customer first.
I compared revenue per customer as well as shares.
I said that a flat result means age is not the lever.
I proposed a different cut to test.

challenges.title: Which device should get the extra search budget?

brief.subject: +30% on Google non-brand search: where should it go?
body: We sell plush toys online. Nearly all paid traffic comes from Google non-brand search, and Finance approved 30% more budget there.

Our agency quotes about $2.50 per click, the same on desktop and mobile. Treat one click as one website session. Use the last 6 months (19 Sep 2014 to 18 Mar 2015): the site changed a lot before that.
Is the extra budget worth it, and on which device? I have five minutes on Friday.
brief.ask: Deliver a three-sentence answer: the call, the evidence, the action.
facts: Channel: utm_source = 'gsearch' and utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'.
The $2.50 click price comes from Maya, not from the database.

questions: What does one click earn after product cost and refunds?
Is that the same on desktop and mobile?
Is the gap real or noise?

frame.nudge: Every click costs money and earns money. What do we earn per click after product cost and refunds, and is that the same for every kind of visitor?
tree: Earn per session vs $2.50 paid per session
Is any gap real or noise, and stable over months?
hyp: Desktop earns more per session than mobile.
Mobile sits below break-even at $2.50, desktop above.
traps: Revenue is not profit: subtract cost of goods and refunds.
Sessions without an order earn $0 but still cost a click: divide by all sessions.
Three years of data mix very different sites: use the recent window.
Text 'NULL' in UTM columns means direct/organic traffic.

tables: Every click is a session; holds channel, campaign and device.
Price and cost per order, linked to the session.
Profit is not revenue: refunds must come off.
Order-level price and cost already sit in orders.
Funnel data; not needed for click economics.
grain: website_sessions: one row per visit. Start here so non-buyers stay.
orders: at most one order per session. LEFT JOIN from sessions.
order_item_refunds: several rows per order for 8 orders. Pre-aggregate per order before joining.
data.goal: One row per device: sessions, orders, conversion rate, revenue and net margin per session.
data.skeleton:
WITH refunds AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT s.device_type
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(____) AS orders          -- which column is NULL when there is no order?
     , ...                            -- conversion rate %
     , ...                            -- net margin per session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON ____
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE ____                            -- channel and 6-month window
GROUP BY s.device_type
data.solution:
WITH refunds AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT s.device_type
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS sessions
     , COUNT(o.order_id)                                 AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(o.order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)    AS cvr_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd) / COUNT(*), 3)             AS revenue_per_session
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd - o.cogs_usd - COALESCE(r.refund_usd, 0)) / COUNT(*), 3) AS net_margin_per_session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE s.utm_source = 'gsearch' AND s.utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'
  AND s.created_at >= '2014-09-19' AND s.created_at < '2015-03-19'
GROUP BY s.device_type
watch: INNER JOIN to orders drops every non-buyer, so conversion reads 100%.
Averaging only over buyers gives margin per order, not per click.
BETWEEN with an end date misses most of the last day on datetimes: use >= and <.

extra_sql.title: Month by month, desktop vs mobile (pivot with conditional aggregation, feeds the line chart)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(s.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(s.created_at) AS yr_month
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'desktop' AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'desktop' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS desktop_cvr
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'mobile' AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'mobile' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS mobile_cvr
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
WHERE s.utm_source = 'gsearch' AND s.utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'
  AND s.created_at >= '2014-09-19' AND s.created_at < '2015-03-19'
GROUP BY YEAR(s.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(s.created_at)
ORDER BY yr_month

metrics: Equals net margin per session: pay less and the click makes money.

viz_specs.title: Desktop clears the $2.50 click price; mobile does not
viz_specs.sub: Net margin per session, 19 Sep 2014 to 18 Mar 2015. Whiskers: 95% CI.
viz_specs.why: Two values against a threshold: bars from zero plus a price line. Whiskers show uncertainty.

viz_specs.title: The gap shows up every month
viz_specs.sub: Conversion rate by month and device. First and last month are partial.
viz_specs.why: Change over time: lines, same colour per device in both charts.

stats.prompt: Desktop converts at 10.2%, mobile at 3.6%. Which approach shows the gap is not luck?
options: Paired t-test
Desktop and mobile are different visits, not pairs.
Two-proportion z-test plus a CI for the difference
Yes/no outcome per session in two independent groups; the CI gives the size of the gap.
Correlation of device and revenue
Device is a category; correlation does not give the gap in business terms.
No test, the chart is obvious
A decision needs an interval you can defend.
read: Desktop's whole interval sits above $2.50. Mobile's sits below. The verdict does not hinge on noise.
Margin intervals use a Welch (unequal variance) interval on session-level margin; with 25k+ sessions per group the normal approximation is fine.
watch: A tiny p-value does not say why. We compared groups; mobile ads may use other keywords or pages.
Most sessions earn $0, so check the interval, not just the mean.

model: Yes for desktop, no for mobile. At $2.50 a click desktop makes money and mobile loses it, so the extra budget should go to desktop only.

A desktop session earns $3.87 net margin (after cost of goods and refunds), a mobile session $1.36. That is $1.37 profit per desktop click and -$1.14 per mobile click. Desktop converts 10.2% of sessions against 3.6% on mobile (gap 6.6 points, 95% CI 6.3 to 6.9) and leads every month.

About 4,029 extra clicks a month on desktop is worth about $5,510 a month, against $2,375 if spread like today. Lower mobile bids below $1.26 a click or pause mobile. Caveat: click price usually rises with volume, so raise desktop bids in steps; we have not tested why mobile converts worse.
checks: My first sentence is the call (yes / no / where).
I used net margin per session over all sessions, not revenue.
I compared each device with the $2.50 click price.
I quoted an interval, and one caveat.

challenges.title: Refunds jumped this summer. Blip or trend, and which product?

brief.subject: Refund rate: is something broken?
body: Refund numbers looked ugly in the autumn review, and I cannot tell whether it is one product, one bad month or a new normal.
Please check May 2014 onward. Define the refund rate as items refunded ÷ items sold, grouped by the month the item was bought.
If something broke, I need to know which product and when, so I can chase the supplier.
brief.ask: Deliver three sentences: which product, how big and for how long, and what Dan should do.
facts: Window: items bought from 1 May 2014 to 19 Mar 2015.
Tables hold items sold (order_items), refunds and the product list.

questions: Which product has an unusual refund rate?
When did the spike start, and did it persist?
Is the spike bigger than the normal ups and downs?

frame.nudge: A rate has a top and a bottom. Which product, which month? Split the overall rate in two directions before you decide anything.
tree: Which product(s) have an unusual rate?
When did it start and does it persist? (month by month)
Is the spike bigger than normal ups and downs?
hyp: One product drives the spike.
The spike is limited to a few months and then returns to normal.
A product can have a high rate without a spike: check both views.
traps: Count refunded items against items sold, not against refund rows or orders.
Group by purchase month; refunds arrive later but belong to the sale.
Compare against the other products in the same months, not against a different period.
The product with the highest overall rate is not necessarily the one with the spike: look at the rate over time as well as the total.

tables: Items sold: product and purchase date.
Header level; items are the right grain for an item rate.
grain: order_items: one row per item sold. This is the denominator.
order_item_refunds: at most one row per refunded item (LEFT JOIN to keep non-refunded items).
products: join for names.
data.goal: Refund rate by product, then by month for the problem product vs all others.
data.skeleton:
SELECT p.product_name
     , COUNT(*) AS items_sold
     , SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN ____ ELSE 0 END) AS items_refunded
     , ...                              -- refund rate %
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN ____ r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= ____
GROUP BY p.product_name
data.solution:
SELECT p.product_name
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS items_sold
     , SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS items_refunded
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS refund_rate_pct
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN order_item_refunds r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= '2014-05-01'
GROUP BY p.product_name
ORDER BY refund_rate_pct DESC
watch: INNER JOIN to refunds keeps only refunded items, so the rate reads 100%.
COUNT(r.order_item_id) and the SUM(CASE...) give the same numerator; pick one and be consistent.
Dividing by orders instead of items changes the rate for multi-item orders.

extra_sql.title: Month-by-month (pivot with conditional aggregation)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(i.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(i.created_at) AS yr_month
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id = 1 AND r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS original_mr_fuzzy
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id <> 1 AND r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id <> 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS other_products
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN order_item_refunds r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= '2014-05-01'
GROUP BY YEAR(i.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(i.created_at)
ORDER BY yr_month

metrics: Items refunded ÷ items sold, by purchase month.
The rate in months without the spike, for the same product.
(Spike rate − baseline) × items sold in the spike months.

viz_specs.title: One product, two months
viz_specs.sub: Refund rate by purchase month, since May 2014.
viz_specs.why: Change over time for two groups: two lines. A table of 11 months would hide the shape.

stats.prompt: Original Mr. Fuzzy: 13.5% refunded in Aug-Sep 2014 vs 3.6% in the other months. Which approach?
options: Two-proportion z-test plus CI on the two periods
Two independent groups of items with a yes/no outcome.
Average the monthly rates and compare means
Months have different volumes; averaging rates ignores that.
Correlation of month number and refund rate
A spike then recovery is not a linear trend.
No test needed
Even a big gap deserves an interval before you chase a supplier.
read: The spike is far outside normal variation, so it is a real event, not noise.
Excess refunds in the two months: about 199 items.
watch: A significant spike says nothing about the cause: batch, supplier, shipping or a listing error.
Two months is a short run: confirm October stayed normal before calling it a blip.

model: It is a blip on one product. The Original Mr. Fuzzy had a refund spike in August and September 2014 and has been back to normal since October.

Its refund rate was 13.5% in those two months against 3.6% in other months (gap 9.9 pts, 95% CI 8.3 to 11.4). Other products stayed flat. Separately, The Birthday Sugar Panda has the highest rate over the whole window (5.8%) with no spike: a steady, higher baseline rather than an event.

No ongoing fix needed. Ask the supplier about Mr. Fuzzy items bought in Aug-Sep 2014 (about 199 extra refunds). Put a review of the Panda's steady rate on the list as a separate item. Caveat: the data does not show the cause; confirm with the refund reasons if Ops has them.
checks: I named the product and the months.
I compared the spike with the product's own baseline.
I said whether it persists.
I gave Dan one next step and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which traffic sources bring buyers?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website.
context.situation: Marketing buys traffic from two search engines (Google, Bing) and ran two small social media pilots. Some visitors arrive with no tag at all: they typed the address or came from an organic search result.
context.decision: Which channels deserve more attention, which look weak, and what do you still need to know before moving budget?

brief.subject: Where do our buyers come from?
body: I read the traffic report every Monday and it ranks channels by visits. The biggest channel is not necessarily the best one. I want a view by channel that shows visits, orders and the order rate.

Use sessions from 1 January 2014, when both social pilots were running or about to run. Split untagged traffic into Direct (no tag, no referrer) and Organic search (no tag, but the visitor came from a search engine).
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which channels convert best, which one looks weak and why you trust that, and what is missing before we move budget.
facts: A session is one visit. An order rate is orders ÷ sessions.
Untagged traffic has the text 'NULL' in utm_source and utm_campaign (a missing value after loading). The shop's search tags are gsearch and bsearch; socialbook is the social media partner.

questions: How many sessions and orders does each channel have?
Which channels convert better or worse than the site average?
How sure are you about the weakest one?

frame.nudge: Visits are not buyers. A channel can be large and average, small and excellent, or small and bad. Which of those do you need to tell apart, and what does a size of 5,000 sessions let you say?
tree: Order rate and revenue per session
Size of the sample behind each rate
What the data does not include (cost)
hyp: Brand search converts better than non-brand search.
The social pilots convert worse than search.
traps: INNER JOIN to orders drops visitors who did not buy and turns every rate into 100%.
Untagged traffic is two things. Direct and organic search behave differently.
Cost per click is not in the data: a high order rate can still be a poor return.

tables: One row per visit: source, campaign, device, whether it is a repeat visit.
One row per order, linked to the session.
Page-level data; not needed for source totals.
Items are inside the order already.
Refunds are covered in another case.
grain: website_sessions: one row per visit. Start here so non-buyers stay.
orders: at most one order per session. LEFT JOIN from sessions, then COUNT(o.order_id) counts only buyers.
data.goal: One row per channel: sessions, orders, order rate and revenue per session, from 1 January 2014.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN (utm_source is empty) AND (http_referer is empty) THEN 'Direct'
            WHEN utm_source is empty THEN 'Organic search'
            ELSE CONCAT(s.utm_source, ' ', s.utm_campaign) END AS channel
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(____) AS orders
     , ...                          -- order rate %, revenue per session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ____
WHERE s.created_at >= ____
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY sessions DESC
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN (s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL') AND (s.http_referer IS NULL OR s.http_referer = 'NULL') THEN 'Direct'
            WHEN s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL' THEN 'Organic search'
            ELSE CONCAT(s.utm_source, ' ', s.utm_campaign) END AS channel
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS sessions
     , COUNT(o.order_id)                                 AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(o.order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)    AS order_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd) / COUNT(*), 2)             AS revenue_per_session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
WHERE s.created_at >= '2014-01-01'
GROUP BY CASE WHEN (s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL') AND (s.http_referer IS NULL OR s.http_referer = 'NULL') THEN 'Direct'
            WHEN s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL' THEN 'Organic search'
            ELSE CONCAT(s.utm_source, ' ', s.utm_campaign) END
ORDER BY sessions DESC
watch: Repeat the CASE in GROUP BY (T-SQL cannot group by the alias).
COUNT(o.order_id) skips NULLs: it counts orders. COUNT(*) counts sessions.

metrics: Order revenue ÷ all sessions, including those that did not buy.
Sessions in the channel. It sets how far a rate can move by chance.

viz_specs.title: Search, organic and direct convert alike at about 7.5%; the social pilots sit far below
viz_specs.sub: Order rate by channel from 1 Jan 2014, with a 95% interval.
viz_specs.why: A rate per category with uncertainty: bars from zero, whiskers for chance, a line for the site average.

model: The big channels convert alike: every channel with more than 20,000 sessions sits between 7.5% and 7.8%. Only bsearch brand is better (9.5%, on a small 5,731 sessions) and the two social media pilots are worse (5.2% and 1.1%).

Non-brand search brings the most visits (164,296 sessions on Google) at 7.5%, about the same as organic search (7.8%) and direct (7.5%), so order rate does not separate them and cost per click will. The first social pilot placed 55 orders from 5,095 sessions; the desktop-targeted one 288 from 5,590. Both are far below the 7.5% site average with enough sessions for the gap to be real, not noise.

Do not move budget on order rate alone. Keep the search channels, pause the first-style social pilot, and fund the desktop-targeted version only if its click price is well under search. Caveat: order rate is not profit, and cost per click by channel is the missing number.
checks: I used a LEFT JOIN from sessions.
I split untagged traffic into direct and organic search.
I read the number of sessions next to each rate.
I said what is missing before moving budget (cost).

challenges.title: Do repeat visitors buy more than first-time visitors?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website.
context.situation: About one visit in six is a repeat visit. The CRM manager wants to fund an email and retargeting program aimed at people who already visited once.
context.decision: Is a repeat visitor worth more than a first-time visitor, and does that hold in every traffic source?

brief.subject: Is a returning visitor worth chasing?
body: The CRM manager says repeat visitors "convert much better" and wants a retargeting budget. I want to see the numbers first.

Compare first visits with repeat visits over all three years: sessions, orders, order rate and average order value. Then check whether the difference holds inside each traffic source, so we know it is more than a source mix.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how much better repeat visitors convert, whether it holds in every source, and what you would do (and not claim).
facts: is_repeat_session = 1 marks a visit by a user who has been to the site before.
Untagged visits ('NULL' source) are direct or organic traffic.

questions: What is the order rate for first visits and for repeat visits?
Do repeat visitors spend more per order?
Is the gap the same in every traffic source?

frame.nudge: A repeat visitor chose to come back. What does that tell you about them before they ever see an email, and what would you need to claim that retargeting causes the difference?
hyp: Repeat visitors convert better by about a point or two.
Order value is about the same.
traps: Comparing two groups does not show that one thing caused the other. Repeat visitors are already interested.
A gap overall can come from source mix. Check inside each source.
Average order value only exists for sessions with an order: divide by orders, not sessions.

tables: One row per visit: source, campaign, device, whether it is a repeat visit.
One row per order, linked to the session.
grain: website_sessions: one row per visit; is_repeat_session splits the groups.
orders: LEFT JOIN from sessions so visits without an order count in the denominator.
data.goal: One row per visit type: sessions, orders, order rate and average order value.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 THEN 'Repeat visit' ELSE 'First visit' END AS visit_type
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(____) AS orders
     , ...                          -- order rate %, average order value
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ____
GROUP BY ____
ORDER BY visit_type
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 THEN 'Repeat visit' ELSE 'First visit' END AS visit_type
     , COUNT(*)                                            AS sessions
     , COUNT(o.order_id)                                   AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(o.order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)      AS order_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd) / COUNT(o.order_id), 2)      AS avg_order_value
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
GROUP BY CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 THEN 'Repeat visit' ELSE 'First visit' END
ORDER BY visit_type
watch: AVG over all sessions would divide revenue by sessions, not by orders. Use SUM / COUNT(order_id).
Check that sessions add up to the table total (472,871).

extra_sql.title: Does the gap hold inside each source? (first visit vs repeat visit rate)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL' THEN 'Untagged' ELSE s.utm_source END AS source
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 0 AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS first_visit_rate
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 2) AS repeat_visit_rate
     , SUM(CASE WHEN s.is_repeat_session = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)           AS repeat_sessions
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
GROUP BY CASE WHEN s.utm_source IS NULL OR s.utm_source = 'NULL' THEN 'Untagged' ELSE s.utm_source END
ORDER BY source

metrics: Compare the same two groups inside each traffic source to see if a gap survives.

viz_specs.title: Repeat visits convert 1.2 points better
viz_specs.sub: Order rate by visit type, all sessions, with a 95% interval.
viz_specs.why: Two groups with uncertainty: bars from zero with whiskers.

viz_specs.title: The gap shows up in every source
viz_specs.sub: Order rate by source and visit type (sources with more than 1,000 repeat visits).
viz_specs.why: Same comparison per segment: paired bars show the gap holds or not.

model: Repeat visitors convert better, 7.8% against 6.6%, but they spend the same per order ($60.54 against $59.86). The gain is a modest 1.2 points.

The gap is 1.2 points (95% interval 1.0 to 1.4) and it holds inside every source with enough repeat visits (between 0.9 and 2.1 points), so source mix does not explain it. Repeat visits are 17% of sessions and 19% of orders.

A modest retargeting test is reasonable, aimed at repeat visitors who left without buying. Do not budget on this comparison alone: repeat visitors already wanted to come back, so it does not show that email or retargeting causes the extra orders. Run a holdout test with a group that gets no retargeting.
checks: I used a LEFT JOIN from sessions.
I checked the gap inside each source.
I did not claim that retargeting causes the gap.
I proposed a holdout test.

challenges.title: Where do visitors drop out on the way to an order?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website.
context.situation: The site team has time for one conversion test next quarter. Several people suggest different pages to improve, each with a good story.
context.decision: Which step in the path from landing page to order is the best candidate for the next test?

brief.from_: Ben Hartley, Head of Site Experience
brief.subject: Which step do we fix first?
body: Visitors land on the site, browse, add to cart, and check out through shipping and billing pages. I can run only one test next quarter and I want to pick the step with the strongest case.

Count the sessions that reached each step: landing page, the products list, a product page, cart, shipping, billing, and the order confirmation page. Give me sessions, the share of the previous step, and the share of all sessions at every step.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: where visitors are lost, which step you would test first, and why the biggest loss may not be the best test.
facts: Use website_pageviews: a session 'reached' a step if it opened that page at least once.
The confirmation page is /thank-you-for-your-order. Product pages are the four product URLs. Billing has two versions: /billing and /billing-2.

questions: How many sessions reach each step?
Which step loses the highest share of visitors, and which loses the highest number?
If you could improve one step by 10%, does it matter which one?

frame.nudge: A funnel has two kinds of 'biggest drop': the largest number lost and the lowest pass rate. Before you look, decide which one you would follow, and what you would still need to know.
tree: Pass rate from one step to the next
What a 10% gain at one step does to orders
hyp: The biggest loss in numbers is the first step after the landing page.
A 10% improvement at any step has the same effect on orders.
traps: A step count is sessions that ever reached the page, not a strict sequence.
A rate of 80% on a huge step may matter less than 45% on a mid-size one.
Steps multiply: improving any step by 10% lifts the final orders by 10%, so the choice is about cost and chance of success.

tables: One row per page opened, with the session and the URL.
Session attributes are not needed to count steps.
The thank-you page marks an order.
grain: website_pageviews: many rows per session. Collapse to one row per session with MAX(CASE WHEN ...) flags first.
Then sum the flags per step and stack the steps with UNION ALL. LAG gives the previous step, FIRST_VALUE the first.
data.goal: One row per step: sessions, share of previous step, share of all sessions.
data.skeleton:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT website_session_id
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/products' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS saw_products
         , ...                      -- product page, cart, shipping, billing, order
    FROM website_pageviews
    GROUP BY ____
),
steps AS (
    SELECT 1 AS step_no, 'Landing page' AS step, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'Products list', SUM(saw_products) FROM s
    UNION ALL ...
)
SELECT step_no, step, sessions
     , ROUND(100.0 * sessions / LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY ____), 1) AS pct_of_previous_step
     , ...                          -- share of all sessions
FROM steps
ORDER BY step_no
data.solution:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT website_session_id
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/products' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                    AS saw_products
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url IN ('/the-original-mr-fuzzy', '/the-forever-love-bear',
                                          '/the-birthday-sugar-panda', '/the-hudson-river-mini-bear') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS saw_product_page
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                        AS saw_cart
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/shipping' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                    AS saw_shipping
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url IN ('/billing', '/billing-2') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                    AS saw_billing
         , MAX(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/thank-you-for-your-order' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                    AS ordered
    FROM website_pageviews
    GROUP BY website_session_id
),
steps AS (
    SELECT 1 AS step_no, 'Landing page' AS step, COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'Products list', SUM(saw_products) FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 3, 'Product page', SUM(saw_product_page) FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 4, 'Cart', SUM(saw_cart) FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 5, 'Shipping', SUM(saw_shipping) FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 6, 'Billing', SUM(saw_billing) FROM s
    UNION ALL SELECT 7, 'Order placed', SUM(ordered) FROM s
)
SELECT step_no
     , step
     , sessions
     , ROUND(100.0 * sessions / LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY step_no), 1)          AS pct_of_previous_step
     , ROUND(100.0 * sessions / FIRST_VALUE(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY step_no), 1)  AS pct_of_all_sessions
FROM steps
ORDER BY step_no
watch: Count a session once per step: use the MAX flag, not COUNT of pageviews.
The first row has no previous step, so its pass rate is NULL by design.

metrics: A session that opened the step's page at least once.
Sessions at this step ÷ sessions at the previous step.
Sessions at the previous step − sessions at this step.

viz_specs.title: Cart has the lowest pass rate: 45%
viz_specs.sub: Share of sessions that continue from the previous step, all sessions.
viz_specs.why: Rates per step in funnel order: bars from zero, the weakest step highlighted.

model: Visitors are lost everywhere, but Cart has the lowest pass rate (45% continue) and Products list comes next (55%). Test one of those two first.

The largest loss in numbers is between the landing page and the products list (211,640 sessions lost), and only 55% of sessions open the products list. Overall 6.8% of 472,871 sessions end in an order. Because steps multiply, a 10% gain at any step is worth the same 3,231 orders, so choose the test that is cheapest to run and most likely to work.

Test a change to the weakest step (for example a clearer cart page) with a 50/50 split, and measure orders per session as well as the pass rate of that step. Caveat: these counts mix three years of a site that changed a lot; rerun on the last six months before you plan.
checks: I counted a session once per step.
I separated pass rate from absolute loss.
I noted that steps multiply.
I proposed a test with a measurable outcome.

challenges.title: The new billing page was tested. Did it win?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website.
context.situation: In September 2012 the shop launched a redesigned billing page, /billing-2, while the old /billing page kept serving some visitors. In January 2013 everyone moved to the new page.
context.decision: Did the new page convert more of the visitors who reached billing, and how sure can we be that it was the page and not the timing?

brief.from_: Ben Hartley, Head of Site Experience
brief.subject: Was the billing page redesign worth it?
body: The redesign has been live for years and nobody wrote up the test. The CEO asks if it paid off. If I say yes, the same team wants to redesign the shipping page next.

Visitors who reached billing were shown one of the two pages. For the weeks when both pages were live (10 September 2012 to 5 January 2013), compare the share of billing sessions that ended in an order and the revenue per billing session. Check first that both pages ran side by side during that window.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which page won, how big the difference is with an interval, and the caveat.
facts: A session reaches billing if it opened /billing or /billing-2. No session saw both.
Orders link to sessions through website_session_id.

questions: Did both pages run in parallel during the window?
What share of billing sessions placed an order on each page?
Is the difference bigger than chance?

frame.nudge: A before/after comparison mixes the page with everything else that changed over time. This case has a better option: both pages ran at the same time. What must be true for that comparison to be fair?
tree: Both pages live in the same weeks
Order rate per billing session on each page
Size of the gap against chance
hyp: The new page converts clearly more.
The two pages ran in roughly equal numbers.
traps: After 5 January 2013 only the new page exists. Do not compare it with the old page's earlier months.
A gap needs the same weeks for both pages, because conversion rises over time anyway.
A significant gap does not say why. The page may differ in several ways.

tables: Which billing page a session saw, and when.
Whether the session ended in an order, and its price.
grain: website_pageviews: many rows per session. Take one row per billing session with MIN(pageview_url) inside the test window.
orders: LEFT JOIN from billing sessions so the sessions without an order stay.
data.goal: One row per billing page: sessions, orders, order rate and revenue per billing session, in the shared window.
data.skeleton:
WITH b AS (
    SELECT website_session_id, MIN(pageview_url) AS billing_page
    FROM website_pageviews
    WHERE pageview_url IN (____)
      AND created_at >= ____
      AND created_at <  ____
    GROUP BY website_session_id
)
SELECT b.billing_page
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(____) AS orders
     , ...                          -- order rate %, revenue per billing session
FROM b
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ____
GROUP BY b.billing_page
data.solution:
WITH b AS (
    SELECT website_session_id, MIN(pageview_url) AS billing_page
    FROM website_pageviews
    WHERE pageview_url IN ('/billing', '/billing-2')
      AND created_at >= '2012-09-10'
      AND created_at <  '2013-01-06'
    GROUP BY website_session_id
)
SELECT b.billing_page
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS sessions
     , COUNT(o.order_id)                                 AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(o.order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)    AS order_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd) / COUNT(*), 2)             AS revenue_per_billing_session
FROM b
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = b.website_session_id
GROUP BY b.billing_page
ORDER BY b.billing_page
watch: BETWEEN with an end date misses the last day on timestamps: use >= and <.
Count orders with COUNT(o.order_id), not COUNT(*).

extra_sql.title: Did both pages run side by side? (billing page views by month)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(created_at) * 100 + MONTH(created_at)                       AS yr_month
     , SUM(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/billing'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS billing_views
     , SUM(CASE WHEN pageview_url = '/billing-2' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS billing2_views
FROM website_pageviews
WHERE pageview_url IN ('/billing', '/billing-2')
  AND created_at >= '2012-09-01'
  AND created_at <  '2013-02-01'
GROUP BY YEAR(created_at) * 100 + MONTH(created_at)
ORDER BY yr_month

metrics: Orders ÷ sessions that reached the billing page.
Order revenue ÷ billing sessions, including those with no order.
The weeks when both pages were live, so time-related changes hit both.

viz_specs.title: The new page converts 62% of billing sessions, the old one 45%
viz_specs.sub: Orders ÷ billing sessions, 10 Sep 2012 to 5 Jan 2013, with a 95% interval.
viz_specs.why: Two groups with uncertainty: bars from zero with whiskers; the intervals do not touch.

viz_specs.title: Both pages were live from September to the first days of January
viz_specs.sub: Billing page views by month. The old page ends in early January 2013.
viz_specs.why: Two series over time: lines show that the pages ran together, then the old page disappears.

stats.prompt: The new page converts 62.1% and the old one 45.1% of billing sessions. Which approach shows the gap is not luck?
options: Paired t-test
The two groups are different visitors, not the same people measured twice.
Two-proportion z-test plus a CI for the difference
Yes or no outcome per session in two independent groups; the CI gives the size of the gap.
Correlation of page and revenue
Page is a category; correlation does not give the gap in business terms.
No test, the gap is obvious
A decision needs an interval you can defend.
read: The whole interval is above zero. The gap is real, not noise.
Both pages had about 1,663 sessions, so the groups are balanced.
watch: The test shows the new page converts better, not which change on it did the work.
Only visitors who reached billing are in the test. Nothing is known about earlier steps.

model: Yes, the new billing page won clearly: 62.1% of billing sessions placed an order against 45.1% on the old page.

Both pages ran side by side from 10 September 2012 to 5 January 2013, with 1,657 and 1,663 billing sessions. The gap is 17.0 points (95% interval 13.7 to 20.3), and a billing session on the new page earns $31.04 against $22.55. Comparing all years would give 63% against 45%: similar, but unfair, because it mixes different periods.

Credit the redesign and run the next test the same way: two versions live in the same weeks, a pre-agreed outcome, and an interval. Caveat: this says the page works better, not which change caused it, and it covers only visitors who reached billing.
checks: I confirmed both pages ran in the same weeks.
I used a LEFT JOIN so non-buyers stay.
I quoted the gap with an interval.
I said what the test cannot show.

challenges.title: Revenue grew every year. Which driver did the work?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website.
context.situation: Revenue roughly doubled or better each year since launch. The leadership team splits next year's plan between traffic, site conversion and basket size, and has no agreed view of what drove the past growth.
context.decision: Which driver explained most of the growth in each year, and did that change?

brief.from_: Ben Hartley, Head of Site Experience
brief.subject: What drove three years of growth?
body: Revenue is up every year and each team says it was them: marketing says traffic, my team says conversion, merchandising says bigger baskets. I want the data to decide.

The data runs from 19 March 2012 to 19 March 2015, which gives three full 12-month periods. Define them as Year 1 (to 18 March 2013), Year 2 (to 18 March 2014) and Year 3 (to 19 March 2015). For each year give sessions, orders, order rate, average order value and revenue.
Then split the growth between Year 1 and 2, and Year 2 and 3, into traffic, order rate and order value.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which driver mattered most in each year, how the picture changed, and what it means for next year's plan.
facts: Revenue = sum of order price_usd. It does not subtract refunds or cost.
Revenue = sessions × order rate × average order value, so growth multiplies across the three drivers.

questions: How did sessions, order rate and order value change each year?
Which driver explains most of the revenue growth in each year?
What does that suggest for next year?

frame.nudge: Revenue is a product of three numbers. How would you decide how much of the growth each one 'owns'? Think in ratios (x times) and logs.
tree: Equal-length years from the first date
Sessions, order rate, order value per year
Share of each driver in the total growth
hyp: Traffic drove most of the growth.
Order rate mattered more in the early years.
traps: Calendar years are uneven here (2012 starts in March, 2015 ends in March). Use 12-month periods.
Revenue growth is multiplicative. Split it with ratios or logs, not by subtracting percentages.
Order value is an average over orders; do not average it over sessions.

tables: One row per visit: source, campaign, device, whether it is a repeat visit.
One row per order, linked to the session.
grain: website_sessions: one row per visit, with its date. Label each session with the business year in a CTE.
orders: LEFT JOIN from sessions. COUNT(order_id) counts orders; SUM(price_usd) / COUNT(order_id) is the average order value.
data.goal: One row per business year: sessions, orders, order rate, average order value and revenue.
data.skeleton:
WITH b AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN s.created_at < '2013-03-19' THEN 'Year 1'
                WHEN ____ THEN 'Year 2'
                ELSE 'Year 3' END AS business_year
         , s.website_session_id, o.order_id, o.price_usd
    FROM website_sessions s
