    LEFT JOIN orders o ON ____
)
SELECT business_year
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(order_id) AS orders
     , ...                          -- order rate %, average order value, revenue
FROM b
GROUP BY business_year
ORDER BY business_year
data.solution:
WITH b AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN s.created_at < '2013-03-19' THEN 'Year 1'
                WHEN s.created_at < '2014-03-19' THEN 'Year 2'
                ELSE 'Year 3' END AS business_year
         , s.website_session_id
         , o.order_id
         , o.price_usd
    FROM website_sessions s
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
)
SELECT business_year
     , COUNT(*)                                       AS sessions
     , COUNT(order_id)                                AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)   AS order_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(price_usd) / COUNT(order_id), 2)     AS avg_order_value
     , ROUND(SUM(price_usd), 0)                       AS revenue
FROM b
GROUP BY business_year
ORDER BY business_year
watch: Do not use YEAR(created_at): calendar years here have different lengths.
Average order value is revenue ÷ orders, never ÷ sessions.

metrics: ln(driver growth factor) ÷ ln(revenue growth factor). The three shares add up to 100%.

viz_specs.title: Traffic grew fastest, but order rate and order value both moved
viz_specs.sub: Index of each driver, previous year = 100.
viz_specs.why: Four ratios in two periods: paired bars against a 100 line show what grew and what did not.

viz_specs.title: In Year 2 conversion did a third of the work; in Year 3 traffic did two thirds
viz_specs.sub: Share of revenue growth explained by each driver.
viz_specs.why: Parts of a whole in two periods: grouped bars compare the shares directly.

model: Traffic was the biggest driver both years, but the mix changed. Between Year 1 and 2 revenue grew x2.68: 55% from traffic, 36% from order rate and 9% from order value.

Between Year 2 and 3 revenue grew x2.51: 69% from traffic, 16% from order rate and 15% from order value. Sessions grew x1.88, while the order rate rose from 6.60% to 7.64% and the average order from $55.50 to $63.79.

Plan on traffic for scale, but remember that the order-rate gains of Year 2 have slowed and the basket gain of Year 3 coincides with new products (the Mini Bear case looks at one of them). Ask each team which of its levers is still unused. Caveat: this is revenue before refunds and cost, and traffic was bought, so traffic growth is not free.
checks: I used equal-length business years.
I split growth with ratios or logs, not by subtracting percentages.
I compared the two periods.
I stated that revenue is not profit.

challenges.title: The Mini Bear launched. New money or cannibalisation?

context.company: Fuzzy Factory is an online shop that sells plush toys. It started with one product, The Original Mr. Fuzzy, in March 2012 and now sells four. All sales happen on its own website. On 5 February 2014 it launched a fourth product, The Hudson River Mini bear, priced at $29.99, the cheapest in the range.
context.situation: Merchandising says the Mini Bear grew the basket. Finance worries it simply replaced sales of the other bears at a lower margin ($20.50 per item against $30 to $37).
context.decision: Did the launch add money to the business, or move money from other products?

brief.from_: Ben Hartley, Head of Site Experience
brief.subject: Mini Bear: add or replace?
body: I want a straight answer for the board. The Mini Bear launched on 5 February 2014. Compare the eight weeks before (11 December 2013 to 4 February 2014) with the eight weeks after (5 February to 1 April 2014): sessions, orders, order rate, items per order, average order value and net margin per session (price minus cost minus refunds, divided by all sessions).
Then look at how items were bought: as the main item of an order or as an add-on. If the Mini Bear is mostly a main item it competes with the other bears. If it is an add-on it adds to the basket.
brief.ask: Reply in four sentences: did the launch add value, how you know it is not replacing other sales, how sure you are, and the caveat that matters most.
facts: is_primary_item = 1 marks the first item in an order; add-ons have 0.
The two windows have the same length (56 days). The before window includes late December.

questions: What changed between the eight weeks before and after?
Is the Mini Bear sold as a main item or as an add-on?
Did add-on sales of the other products fall?

frame.nudge: A before/after comparison can show a change, but it cannot show cause by itself. Which other explanations would you list (season, traffic, other launches), and how could the item-level data help rule one out?
tree: Order rate, items per order and margin per session before and after
What else changed in the same weeks
hyp: Basket size rose but the order rate did not.
The Mini Bear is sold only as an add-on, so it cannot replace a main item.
traps: Equal windows matter: eight weeks against eight weeks, not eight weeks against a year.
Average order value can rise while profit falls. Use net margin per session.
Late December is in the before window: conversion may be seasonally high there.

tables: One row per visit: source, campaign, device, whether it is a repeat visit.
One row per order, linked to the session.
One row per item in an order, with primary-item flag, price and cost.
Product names for the item-level cut.
grain: website_sessions LEFT JOIN orders: one row per visit with at most one order. Refunds must be summed per order before joining.
order_items: one row per item. Split main items and add-ons with is_primary_item.
data.goal: One row per period: sessions, orders, order rate, items per order, average order value and net margin per session.
data.skeleton:
WITH r AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds GROUP BY order_id
),
x AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN s.created_at >= '2013-12-11' AND s.created_at < '2014-02-05' THEN '1. Before (8 weeks)'
                ELSE '2. After (8 weeks)' END AS period
         , s.website_session_id, o.order_id, o.items_purchased, o.price_usd, o.cogs_usd, r.refund_usd
    FROM website_sessions s
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON ____
    LEFT JOIN r ON ____
    WHERE s.created_at >= '2013-12-11' AND s.created_at < '2014-04-02'
)
SELECT period, COUNT(*) AS sessions, COUNT(order_id) AS orders
     , ...                          -- order rate, items per order, average order value
     , ...                          -- net margin per session (all sessions)
FROM x
GROUP BY period
data.solution:
WITH r AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds
    GROUP BY order_id
),
x AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN s.created_at >= '2013-12-11' AND s.created_at < '2014-02-05' THEN '1. Before (8 weeks)'
                ELSE '2. After (8 weeks)' END AS period
         , s.website_session_id, o.order_id, o.items_purchased, o.price_usd, o.cogs_usd, r.refund_usd
    FROM website_sessions s
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
    LEFT JOIN r        ON r.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE s.created_at >= '2013-12-11' AND s.created_at < '2014-04-02'
)
SELECT period
     , COUNT(*)                                                           AS sessions
     , COUNT(order_id)                                                    AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)                       AS order_rate_pct
     , ROUND(1.0 * SUM(items_purchased) / COUNT(order_id), 3)             AS items_per_order
     , ROUND(SUM(price_usd) / COUNT(order_id), 2)                         AS avg_order_value
     , ROUND(SUM(price_usd - cogs_usd - COALESCE(refund_usd, 0)) / COUNT(*), 3) AS net_margin_per_session
FROM x
GROUP BY period
ORDER BY period
watch: Net margin per session divides by all sessions, not by orders.
If you join refunds without summing them per order, an order with two refunds is counted twice.

stats.prompt: The order rate moved from 6.83% to 6.52%. Is the change in order rate larger than chance?
options: Two-proportion z-test plus a CI for the difference
Two independent groups of sessions with a yes or no outcome.
Compare the two numbers by eye
A 0.3-point change on 26 to 31 thousand sessions needs an interval.
Paired t-test
The sessions in the two windows are different visits.
No test needed because AOV rose
AOV and order rate are different questions.
read: The order-rate change sits close to zero. The data does not show that the launch changed how many visits end in an order.
The gain is in items per order: 1.13 before, 1.34 after.
watch: Season, traffic mix and other changes differ between the windows. This is an association, not an experiment.

model: The data points to added money, not replacement. Items per order rose from 1.13 to 1.34 and net margin per session from $2.31 to $2.53 (9%).

All 412 Mini Bears sold in the window were add-ons and none was a main item, so it cannot take a main sale from another bear. Add-ons of the other products rose too, from 229 to 268. The order rate was 6.83% before and 6.52% after (gap -0.31 points, 95% interval -0.72 to 0.11), so the launch did not bring more orders, only fuller ones.

The Mini Bear brought about $8.4K of margin over eight weeks (about 11% of the margin in the after window), with a refund rate of 1.3%. Caveat: the before window includes late December, traffic and season differ, and this is a comparison of periods, not an experiment. A holdout (hide the add-on for some visitors) would settle it.

I compared the order rate and the basket separately.
I split main items from add-ons.

challenges.title: The 2018 promotion: did it bring members who stay?

brief.subject: 2018 promotion: is it working?
body: In 2018 we ran a promotion that enrolled 971 members. The dashboard says 11.8% of them have cancelled against 12.4% of standard members, so I am told the promotion is as good as standard enrollment.
I want to repeat it next year. Is the comparison fair, and are promo members as loyal as standard ones?
brief.ask: Deliver three sentences: is the dashboard comparison right, what is the real picture, what should Ana do.
facts: Churn = member has a cancellation year.
Tables: ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History (one row per member).

questions: Is the dashboard comparing like with like?
What is the churn rate when both groups joined in the same year?
Is the gap bigger than chance?

frame.nudge: Who are the 'standard' members being compared against? When did they join, and for how long have they had the chance to cancel?
tree: Is the promotion as good as standard?
What does the dashboard compare, and is it like for like?
What is churn when both groups joined in the same year?
Is the difference bigger than chance?
hyp: Standard members include years of older enrollments with more time to cancel.
Compared within 2018, promo members cancel much more often.
traps: Members who enrolled in 2012 had six more years to cancel than members who enrolled in 2018.
Compare groups with the same exposure time: filter to the same enrollment year.
An overall average hides the cohort mix.

tables: Has enrollment type, enrollment year and cancellation year per member.
Flight behavior; not needed to measure churn.
Date dimension; years are already on the member row.
grain: ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History: one row per member.
Cancelled = Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL.
Enrollment_Type has two values: Standard and 2018 Promotion.
data.goal: Churn rate by enrollment type, first overall (the dashboard), then within the same enrollment year.
data.skeleton:
-- The dashboard view (all years)
SELECT Enrollment_Type
     , COUNT(*) AS members
     , SUM(CASE WHEN ____ IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
     , ...                    -- cancel rate %
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Type

-- The fair view: add Enrollment_Year to the GROUP BY
data.solution:
SELECT Enrollment_Year
     , Enrollment_Type
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS members
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_rate_pct
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Year, Enrollment_Type
ORDER BY Enrollment_Year, Enrollment_Type

pre.title: The dashboard view (all years)
pre.sql:

     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS members
     , SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS cancelled
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_rate_pct
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Type

watch: The first query reproduces the dashboard: it is correct arithmetic and the wrong comparison.
Promo members exist only for 2018, so the like-for-like check is the 2018 row pair.

metrics: Members with a cancellation year ÷ members.
All members who enrolled in the same year.
Compare promo and standard within enrollment year 2018 only.

viz_specs.title: Fair comparison: promo members cancel five times as often
viz_specs.sub: Cancel rate by enrollment type. The 'All enrollees' bars are the dashboard comparison.
viz_specs.why: Two groups in two scopes: grouped bars. The jump between the scopes is the story.

stats.prompt: Promo vs standard members enrolled in 2018 (yes/no: cancelled). Which approach?
options: Two-proportion z-test plus CI on 2018 enrollees
Two independent groups with a yes/no outcome, same enrollment year.
Two-proportion z-test on all members
That repeats the unfair comparison with a p-value on top.
Paired t-test
Members are different people, not pairs.
Compare the means of CLV
CLV is a different question from cancellation.
read: Within 2018 the gap is large and the interval is far from 0.
Ratio: promo cancel rate is about 5.5x the standard rate in the same cohort.
watch: Promo members may differ in other ways (offer, channel, age). This is a comparison, not an experiment.
Cancellation is counted to date: both groups had the same exposure, so the comparison is fair, but the absolute rates will rise.

model: No. Promo members are much less loyal, and the dashboard hid it by comparing them with older standard members who had years longer to cancel.

Overall, 11.8% of promo and 12.4% of standard members cancelled. Within the 2018 cohort, where both groups had the same time, promo members cancelled at 11.8% vs 2.2% (gap 9.7 pts, 95% CI 7.6 to 11.8).

Do not repeat the promotion as designed. Test a version with a retention hook (for example a second-year benefit) and compare it with standard members from the same month. Caveat: promo members may differ in other ways; a randomized test would settle it.
checks: I explained why the dashboard comparison is unfair.
I compared groups within the same enrollment year.
I quoted the gap and its interval.
I proposed a next test.
